carousel.body: State the business plan explicitly, including the numbers. You cannot find hidden assumptions in a strategy that exists only as a shared feeling in the room.

carousel.title: Invert to assumptions
carousel.body: Ask what would have to be true for these numbers to happen. List them plainly: demand, price, cost, channel, and speed of adoption.

carousel.title: Rank by lethality
carousel.body: Order the assumptions by how badly the venture dies if each one is wrong. Comfortable assumptions get tested first in most companies, which is backwards.

carousel.title: Test the cheapest killer
carousel.body: Spend money on the smallest possible test of the most dangerous assumption. A plan that changes after that test has done its job, not failed.

sparks.hook: A separate business needs separate metrics or it gets strangled politely.
sparks.insight: Small ventures inside large companies die from resource allocation rather than from bad ideas. Against the core business, a new venture always looks worse: lower margins, a smaller market, more uncertainty. If it is judged by the same criteria and competes for the same budget, competent managers will starve it every year for entirely defensible reasons. Autonomy over its own numbers, and often a separate organisation, is the only reliable protection it has.
sparks.why: The criteria an organisation uses to prioritise are harder to change than its processes or its resources. Structural separation works because it removes the comparison rather than trying to win it.
sparks.apply: Give your new venture its own budget, targets and reporting line, and forbid comparing its margin to the core business for two years.

sparks.hook: The size of the market you need decides where you can look.
sparks.insight: A big company genuinely cannot get excited about a small market, because the same effort applied to the existing business produces more. That is not a failure of imagination, it is arithmetic. It does mean, though, that the growth a large firm needs will not be found by scanning the markets it can already see clearly. Either you enter early and grow with a small market, or you pay a large premium later to buy somebody who did.
sparks.why: Large firms face a genuine numbers problem, which is one reason acquiring proven entrants is often rational. The theory's own prescriptions have a mixed record: Christensen's disruption-based investment fund performed poorly and closed early.
sparks.apply: Compare the smallest market your company would approve with the size of the markets your future competitors are entering today.

sparks.hook: Integrate where the product is not good enough, specialise where it is.
sparks.insight: Early in a market, when the technology barely works, controlling the whole stack is an advantage: the pieces must be tuned to each other and the interfaces are not yet stable. Once performance overshoots what customers need, modular architectures win because they allow speed, choice and lower cost. Firms get into trouble by holding an integrated model long after the market stopped rewarding it, or by outsourcing early while the interfaces are still moving.
sparks.why: The link between performance shortfall and architecture is one of the more empirically grounded parts of the argument, visible in computing, cars and phones. Timing the transition remains the hard, unresolved part.
sparks.apply: Ask whether your customers are still short of performance or already have more than they use, then check your make-or-buy decisions match the answer.

sparks.hook: Watch for the moment good enough arrives. It changes who wins.
sparks.insight: Markets flip when the mainstream product exceeds what typical customers can actually use. Before that point buyers pay for performance and the best engineering wins. After it, the extra capability is worth nothing to them and they start choosing on price, convenience or customisation instead. Companies that miss this transition keep investing in improvements customers have quietly stopped valuing, while cheaper rivals take the volume away from them.
sparks.why: Overshoot is observable in most maturing technology categories. The forecasting difficulty is real: the point where performance stops mattering is usually only obvious in hindsight, which limits how actionable this is.
sparks.apply: Ask ten customers which recent improvements they actually use. If most say none, shift investment from performance toward price or convenience.

actions: List every customer segment your company declines as too small or low margin, and find out who serves them now and how fast those rivals are improving.
Interview ten recent buyers about the hour before they started looking, and rewrite your segmentation around situations rather than customer types.
Give one new venture its own budget, targets and reporting line, and set it a profitability milestone before any revenue milestone.
Write the three assumptions your newest initiative would die without, rank them by damage, and spend a month testing only the most dangerous one.
books.not_for_you_if: You want practical steps for a small company, since this is written for corporate strategists and is denser and more theoretical than its famous predecessor.

verification.notes: Published 2003 by Harvard Business School Press, the sequel to The Innovator's Dilemma. Disruption theory has drawn substantial criticism, including Jill Lepore's 2014 essay and a 2015 MIT Sloan review by King and Baatartogtokh. All prose here is original.

books.title: The Lean Startup
books.subtitle: How Today's Entrepreneurs Use Continuous Innovation to Create Radically Successful Businesses
books.author: Eric Ries
books.why_it_matters: It replaced the business plan with the experiment as the basic unit of startup work, and gave a whole industry its shared vocabulary. Corporate innovation teams, accelerators and product organisations still run on the loop it popularised.

crux.headline: Progress is learning, not shipping
crux.body: A new venture is not a small version of a company. It is an organisation searching for a business model under real uncertainty, which means its output is not features but answers. The discipline is to identify the belief your plan most depends on, build the smallest thing that tests it, measure what actually happened rather than what you hoped, and then decide honestly whether to change direction or continue.

sparks.hook: Shipping a lot is not progress if nobody wanted any of it.
sparks.insight: Teams measure themselves by output because output is visible and satisfying: features released, tickets closed, hours worked. Under genuine uncertainty that measure is worthless, because you can execute a plan flawlessly and build something nobody wants. The alternative unit of progress is what you now know that you did not know last month, backed by evidence rather than by opinion. It is a much less comfortable measure, since a productive month can end with the conclusion that the original idea was wrong.
sparks.why: The reframing matters because it changes what gets rewarded. Teams graded on shipping will ship. Teams graded on validated answers will ask better questions and kill weak ideas earlier.
sparks.apply: At the end of this month, write what you learned rather than what you shipped. If the list is empty, you ran no real experiments.

sparks.hook: Your plan rests on two beliefs. Everything else is detail.
sparks.insight: Under the whole business case sit a small number of assumptions that have to be true or nothing works. Two matter most: whether people will actually get value from the thing once they use it, and whether you have a repeatable way for more of them to arrive. Everything else in the plan is derived from those. Naming them explicitly is uncomfortable, because it exposes how much of a confident forecast is resting on a belief nobody has tested and everyone has been assuming.
sparks.why: Isolating the load-bearing assumptions tells you what to test first. Most teams test the safe assumptions because those experiments are pleasant and the results are reassuring.
sparks.apply: Write the two assumptions your plan cannot survive without, then design one cheap test for whichever of them you have the least evidence for.

sparks.hook: Build the smallest thing that could prove you wrong.
sparks.insight: The first version is not a small product. It is an instrument for answering one question, and it should contain nothing that does not serve that question. Sometimes it is a rough product, sometimes a page describing something that does not exist yet, sometimes a service delivered by hand behind the scenes. The bar is not quality or completeness but whether the result would change your mind. If a positive result and a negative result would both lead you to carry on regardless, you have not designed a test.
sparks.why: The concept is widely misused as an excuse for shipping something poor. The real criterion is informational: the smallest build that produces a decision, which is often smaller and sometimes larger than a rough product.
sparks.apply: Before your next build, write the result that would make you abandon the idea. If you cannot write it, redesign the test rather than the product.

sparks.hook: The loop only pays off if you run it faster than your competitors think.
sparks.insight: The cycle is simple to state and hard to run: turn an idea into something you can put in front of people, measure what they do with it, learn from the result, and start again. The advantage comes from the time it takes you to go round once. A team that completes the loop weekly will out-learn a team that completes it quarterly regardless of who is smarter, because they get more chances to be wrong cheaply. So the thing to optimise is not any single stage but the total time from question to answer.
sparks.why: Learning rate compounds in the same way that interest does. Halving your cycle time doubles the number of wrong turns you can afford before running out of money.
sparks.apply: Measure how many days pass between forming a question and having data on it. Cut that number in half before adding anything to the roadmap.

carousel.title: Start from the question
carousel.body: Write the specific uncertainty you are resolving, not the feature you want to build. A vague question produces a build that cannot fail and therefore teaches nothing.

carousel.title: Build only the instrument
carousel.body: Include what is needed to get an answer and nothing else. Every extra piece adds time to the loop and makes it harder to attribute the result to any one thing.

carousel.title: Measure behaviour
carousel.body: Watch what people do rather than what they say. Stated intent is a poor predictor, so design the test so that the answer shows up in an action.

carousel.title: Decide in the open
carousel.body: Write the conclusion down and state whether you are continuing or changing direction. Undocumented results quietly become whatever the loudest person remembers.

sparks.hook: Any metric that only ever goes up is telling you nothing.
sparks.insight: Total registered users, cumulative downloads and total revenue all rise with time regardless of whether the product is improving, which makes them comforting and useless. What tells you something is comparing groups of customers who arrived at different times: does the batch that joined last month behave better than the batch from three months ago? If later groups behave the same as earlier ones, your product changes are not working, however impressive the headline totals look on a chart.
sparks.why: Cumulative numbers hide the direction of travel because they cannot decrease. Splitting by arrival date is one of the few analyses that will actually contradict a team that wants to keep going.
sparks.apply: Rebuild your main dashboard so every number is a rate or a comparison between customer groups, and delete every cumulative total from it.

sparks.hook: A change of direction is a result, not a confession of failure.
sparks.insight: When the evidence says the current approach is not working, the choice is to change one major element of the plan while keeping what you have learned, or to keep going. Both are legitimate, and the common failure is not choosing at all: teams drift, changing small things repeatedly while the central assumption stays untested. Deciding on a schedule rather than in a crisis makes it a normal act of management. It also means the decision is made while there is still money left to act on it.
sparks.why: The word has been stretched to cover any change of plan, which drains it of meaning. The useful version is specific: keep one part of the model, change another, and be able to say which.
sparks.apply: Put a recurring date in the calendar for a persevere-or-change meeting, and require the team to bring evidence rather than opinions to it.

carousel.title: Gather the evidence
carousel.body: Bring cohort data, not anecdotes. The question is whether later customers behave better than earlier ones, because that is what shows whether your work is landing.

carousel.title: Name what changes
carousel.body: Decide which single element moves: the customer, the problem, the channel, the pricing, the technology. Changing everything at once is a restart, not a change of direction.

carousel.title: Keep the learning
carousel.body: Write down what you now know to be true regardless of direction. The value of the last six months is in that list, and it is easily thrown away in a reset.

carousel.title: Set the next checkpoint
carousel.body: Agree the evidence and the date that would trigger the next decision. Without a fixed checkpoint, persevering becomes the default by inertia rather than by choice.

sparks.hook: Small batches feel slower and finish sooner.
sparks.insight: Working in large chunks feels efficient because you set up once and process everything at once. In practice it delays feedback, hides defects until late, and means a mistake made at the start contaminates the entire batch. Shrinking the batch size means work reaches the point of judgement quickly, errors surface while they are cheap, and the queue of half-finished work stops growing. It borrows directly from manufacturing, where the same counter-intuitive result has been demonstrated for decades.
sparks.why: The mechanism is that large batches push discovery of problems to the end, when the cost of fixing them is highest. Small batches trade a little setup overhead for much earlier information.
sparks.apply: Take your largest piece of unreleased work and split it into pieces you can put in front of a real user within a week each.

sparks.hook: Fix the fifth cause, not the first. The first one is never the problem.
sparks.insight: When something breaks, the immediate cause is usually technical and the real cause is usually organisational. Asking why repeatedly moves you from the symptom to a training gap, a missing check, a rushed release process. The discipline is to make a proportionate investment at each level rather than a heroic fix at the surface. Done badly this becomes a search for someone to blame, which is why it only works where the person closest to the failure is the one running the analysis.
sparks.why: Repeated questioning is a crude but effective way to get past the first satisfying explanation. Its weakness is assuming a single causal chain when real failures often have several.
sparks.apply: At your next incident review, ask why five times in a row and commit to one small fix at each level rather than a single large one at the end.

sparks.hook: Optimising a small idea very efficiently is still a small idea.
sparks.insight: The most serious objection is that constant testing pulls you towards local improvement. Each experiment measures a small change against the current state, so the method reliably improves what exists and rarely produces something genuinely new. Several prominent investors have made this argument: some of the largest companies of the last two decades were built by people who committed to a long, unpopular bet that no early experiment could have validated. The method is strong on avoiding waste and weak on generating ambition.
sparks.why: Incremental testing cannot evaluate a proposition whose value only appears at scale or after years of building. Knowing which type of bet you are making tells you whether this toolkit applies at all.
sparks.apply: Ask whether your idea's value would show up in a small test. If it would not, set a milestone and a budget instead of an experiment.

sparks.hook: Speed is worthless if you are pointed at the wrong customer.
sparks.insight: A fast loop applied to the wrong question just gets you to a wrong answer sooner. The choice of who you are serving and what problem you are solving sits above the method and is not itself an experimental output. Teams often iterate energetically for a year inside a market they picked casually, improving conversion on a page that should never have existed. Before optimising the cycle, spend real time on the judgement call about which market and which problem, because that choice bounds everything the loop can achieve.
sparks.why: Experimentation optimises within a frame it cannot choose. This is the most common practical failure of the method: excellent process running on an unexamined premise.
sparks.apply: Write one page justifying your choice of customer and problem, and have someone outside the team argue against it before you plan another sprint.

actions: Write the two assumptions your business cannot survive without, and design one cheap test for whichever you have the least evidence for.
Measure the number of days between forming a question and holding data on it, then halve that number before adding anything new to the roadmap.
Rebuild your main dashboard so that every figure is a rate or a comparison between customer groups, and remove every cumulative total.
Book a recurring persevere-or-change meeting and require the team to bring cohort evidence rather than opinions to it.
books.not_for_you_if: You are making a long-horizon bet whose value cannot appear in a small test, or you want depth on strategy rather than on process.

verification.notes: Published 2011 by Crown Business. The method has been widely criticised for encouraging incremental improvement over ambitious bets. All prose here is original.

books.title: The Toyota Way
books.subtitle: 14 Management Principles from the World's Greatest Manufacturer
books.author: Jeffrey K. Liker
books.why_it_matters: It explained the Toyota production system as a management philosophy rather than a toolkit, which is exactly the distinction most companies copying it got wrong. It remains the clearest account of why the tools fail without the culture underneath.

crux.headline: The tools are the easy part. The culture is the system
crux.body: Anyone can install cards on a board, hold stand-up meetings and label the storage bins. What cannot be installed is an organisation that stops work to fix a small problem, promotes leaders who understand the work from having done it, and accepts a worse quarter to protect a better decade. Companies that copied the visible mechanisms without that foundation got the vocabulary and none of the results, which is the most repeated failure in modern operations.

sparks.hook: Every other principle depends on being willing to lose money this quarter.
sparks.insight: The foundation is a willingness to make decisions on a long horizon even when they damage short-term financial results. That sounds like a platitude until you see what it licenses: refusing to lay off skilled workers in a downturn because rebuilding that knowledge takes a decade, investing in suppliers who are not yet good enough, stopping production over a defect that a customer would probably never notice. None of that survives in a company that is optimised quarter by quarter, which is why the rest of the system rarely transplants.
sparks.why: Every practice downstream costs money in the short run and pays back over years. Without the willingness to absorb that gap, an organisation adopts the cheap visible parts and drops the expensive ones.
sparks.apply: Identify one decision you are making for this quarter's numbers that you would reverse on a ten-year horizon, and reverse it.

sparks.hook: Inventory is not a buffer. It is a blanket over your problems.
sparks.insight: Large stocks of unfinished work look like prudence and function as concealment. If a step is unreliable, a big pile in front of the next step means nobody notices for weeks. Shrink the pile and the unreliability becomes visible immediately and painfully, which is the entire point. Reducing batch sizes and moving toward one-piece flow is not primarily about saving storage cost; it is a deliberate way of removing the cushion so that problems surface while they are still small enough to understand.
sparks.why: Queues decouple steps and hide the variation between them. Removing the queue forces the underlying problem into view, which is uncomfortable and is the only way it gets fixed.
sparks.apply: Halve the batch size in one part of your process and watch what breaks first. Fix that rather than restoring the buffer.

sparks.hook: Build what the next step just took, not what the forecast said.
sparks.insight: A push system makes things according to a plan written in advance and hopes demand cooperates. A pull system makes something only when the step downstream has consumed the previous one, so the actual rate of consumption sets the rate of production. The difference shows up as cash: push systems accumulate stock nobody ordered, absorb capital and then need discounting to clear. Pull systems carry less, respond faster to real changes in demand, and reveal forecasting errors within days rather than at the end of a season.
sparks.why: Forecasts are wrong in proportion to how far ahead they reach. Pull replaces a long-range prediction with a short-range signal, which is a strictly better source of information.
sparks.apply: Pick one internal handoff and switch it to a pull signal: the downstream team requests work rather than the upstream team pushing it.

sparks.hook: Uneven workload does as much damage as outright waste.
sparks.insight: Most improvement programmes hunt only for obvious waste: the wasted motion, the redundant step, the idle wait. Two other problems cause at least as much harm and are usually invisible. Overburden pushes people and equipment beyond safe limits, producing errors, breakdowns and burnout. Unevenness, the peaks and troughs of a lumpy schedule, forces you to staff for the peak and pay for it in the trough. Smoothing the load often removes more waste than attacking waste directly ever will.
sparks.why: Waste, overburden and unevenness are linked: unevenness creates overburden at the peaks, and overburden generates waste through errors and rework. Levelling the schedule attacks the cause rather than the symptom.
sparks.apply: Plot the past twelve weeks of your team's incoming work. If it is lumpy, smooth the release schedule before hiring or adding tooling.

sparks.hook: Let anyone halt the whole line, and quality goes up rather than down.
sparks.insight: Giving every worker the authority to stop production over a defect sounds like a recipe for chaos and paralysis. In practice it produces the opposite, because it makes problems immediate and public rather than deferred and deniable. A stoppage costs minutes now; the same defect discovered by a customer costs a recall and a reputation. The deeper effect is cultural: when stopping is expected rather than punished, people report problems early, and the organisation gets a stream of small correctable faults instead of occasional catastrophes.
sparks.why: Quality inspected at the end can only sort good from bad. Quality built in requires the ability to stop at the moment of the fault, which requires that stopping is genuinely safe for the person doing it.
sparks.apply: Give one team explicit authority to halt a release or a shipment over a quality concern, and publicly back the first person who uses it.

sparks.hook: You cannot improve a process that is done differently every time.
sparks.insight: Standardised work is often heard as bureaucracy imposed on skilled people, and done badly that is exactly what it becomes. Done properly it is the opposite: a written best-known method that anyone doing the work can challenge and change, which then becomes the new standard. The purpose is measurement. Without a stable baseline you cannot tell whether a change helped, so improvement becomes a matter of opinion and the loudest person wins. The standard exists to be replaced, and the people doing the work own it.
sparks.why: Improvement requires a controlled comparison. A process that varies freely produces noise, and in noise every change can be defended and none can be evaluated.
sparks.apply: Write down the current best-known method for one recurring task, then let the people doing it propose the first revision within a month.

sparks.hook: Go and look yourself. A report is someone else's summary of what happened.
sparks.insight: Managers routinely decide about work they have never watched, using numbers assembled by people with a stake in how the numbers look. Going to where the work actually happens and observing it directly gives you information that no dashboard contains: the workaround everyone has adopted, the machine that is fine except on Mondays, the form nobody fills in properly because it makes no sense. This is not a symbolic visit. It means standing there long enough to see the process run several times without interrupting it.
sparks.why: Summaries lose exactly the anomalies that matter, because summarising means discarding the unusual. Direct observation is the only reliable way to recover them.
sparks.apply: Spend two hours this month watching your team's most important process run, taking notes and asking nothing until the end.

sparks.hook: Keep asking why until you reach something you can actually change.
sparks.insight: Most problem-solving stops at the first plausible cause, which is usually a person who made a mistake. Continuing to ask why moves you past the individual and into the system that made the mistake likely: the ambiguous instruction, the tool that fails silently, the schedule that guaranteed someone would be rushing. The number of questions is not sacred; what matters is continuing until you find a cause that is inside your control and whose removal would prevent recurrence rather than merely punishing this occurrence.
sparks.why: Stopping early produces blame and no fix, because the same conditions remain in place for the next person. Systemic causes are less satisfying to identify and are the only ones worth acting on.
sparks.apply: Take last month's worst error and write the chain of causes until you reach one you can change. Change it and record the date.

carousel.title: Describe what happened
carousel.body: Write the observable facts before any interpretation: what was produced, when it was noticed, what it cost. Explanations offered in the first five minutes are almost always wrong.

carousel.title: Go and see the conditions
carousel.body: Look at the actual workstation, code path or document. Reconstructing an incident from memory in a meeting room reliably produces a tidy story that never happened.

carousel.title: Ask why past the person
carousel.body: Each answer becomes the next question. The moment an answer names an individual rather than a condition, ask what made that behaviour the sensible thing to do.

carousel.title: Change one condition
carousel.body: Pick a cause inside your control and alter it, then check weeks later whether the problem recurred. A countermeasure that is never verified is just a meeting outcome.

sparks.hook: Decide slowly with everyone, then implement faster than anyone.
sparks.insight: Spending weeks circulating a proposal, gathering objections and revising it before any formal decision looks painfully slow to organisations that prize decisiveness. The trade is deliberate. By the time the decision is made, every objection has been heard, every affected group has contributed, and implementation meets almost no resistance. The alternative, a fast decision followed by months of quiet obstruction and rework, is usually slower end to end while feeling more dynamic on the day it is announced.
sparks.why: Total elapsed time includes implementation, not just the decision. Front-loading disagreement moves the friction to the cheapest point, before anyone has built anything.
sparks.apply: Before your next significant decision, circulate the proposal to everyone affected and require each to submit one objection in writing.

sparks.hook: Grow your leaders inside, or import someone who will change the answer.
sparks.insight: Organisations under pressure hire senior leaders from outside for their track record, and often get a competent person who does not understand what made this particular place work. A system built on deep knowledge of the actual work requires leaders who have done that work and absorbed the philosophy over years, which means promoting from within is a structural requirement rather than a sentimental preference. The cost is real: internal development is slow, and the pipeline has to be built long before you need it.
sparks.why: Where advantage lives in accumulated practice rather than in strategy documents, an outsider cannot bring it and can unintentionally dismantle it while making sensible-looking changes.
sparks.apply: Name your successor and the two people behind them, then give each a stretch assignment this year that develops the gap you identified.

sparks.hook: Respect means giving people hard problems, not making them comfortable.
sparks.insight: Respect for people is easily misread as a pleasant workplace with good benefits. What it means here is harder and more flattering: assume the people doing the work are the ones who understand it, give them genuinely difficult problems, teach them the method, and then expect them to solve things rather than escalate them. The same logic extends outward to suppliers, who get demanding targets, long relationships and real technical help rather than an annual auction on price.
sparks.why: Honest caveat: the record is not spotless. Toyota's large safety recalls around 2009 and 2010 raised serious questions about whether rapid global growth had outrun the system, and many Western lean programmes have copied the tools while producing none of the results.
sparks.apply: Give one team a problem you would normally solve for them, plus the method and a deadline, and resist providing the answer.

carousel.title: Start with the philosophy
carousel.body: Agree what the organisation is for on a ten-year view. Every later practice costs money in the short run, so without this the programme is cancelled at the first bad quarter.

carousel.title: Fix the process next
carousel.body: Create flow, level the load and make problems visible. This is the layer most companies buy consultants for and the only one they usually implement.

carousel.title: Develop people and partners
carousel.body: Grow leaders internally, teach the method rather than the tools, and treat suppliers as long-term participants who deserve help rather than annual price pressure.

carousel.title: Make problem-solving continuous
carousel.body: Go and see, ask why past the person, reflect honestly on what went wrong, and keep improving in small increments forever rather than in occasional programmes.

actions: Pick one process and cut its batch size or queue in half, then fix the first problem that surfaces instead of restoring the buffer.
Spend two hours observing your most important process directly, writing down every workaround people have quietly invented to make it work.
Run a proper root-cause session on your worst recent failure, continuing past the first person named until you reach a condition you can change.
Name the long-term decision your current quarterly targets are pushing you to get wrong, and take it to your leadership team with the ten-year case.
books.not_for_you_if: You work in a small service business with no repeatable process, or you want a short toolkit rather than a long account of manufacturing culture.

verification.notes: Published 2004 by McGraw-Hill. Liker is a professor of industrial engineering who has studied Toyota since the 1980s. A second edition appeared in 2021. All prose original.

books.title: This Is Marketing
books.subtitle: You Can't Be Seen Until You Learn to See
books.author: Seth Godin
books.why_it_matters: It reframed marketing as the work of understanding a specific group well enough to make something they want, rather than the work of persuading strangers. That framing now shapes how most modern founders and independent creators think about finding an audience.

crux.headline: Marketing is serving a specific someone, not persuading everyone
crux.body: Start with the smallest group you could possibly serve and understand what they already want, believe and fear. Build something that moves them toward it, then earn the right to be heard by showing up consistently over a long period. Growth comes from those people telling others, which only happens if the thing genuinely changed something for them. Attention is not the goal, and it is not for sale in any way that lasts.

sparks.hook: Marketing is not what you say. It is who you decide to serve.
sparks.insight: Most marketing effort goes into wording — the headline, the campaign, the channel. That is the last five percent. The decisions that actually determine whether anything works happen earlier: who exactly this is for, what they are already trying to achieve, and what they will have to give up to switch to you. Get those right and the wording becomes almost obvious. Get them wrong and no amount of clever copy rescues it, because you are talking fluently to people who do not want the thing.
sparks.why: Copy can only amplify a fit that already exists. When the audience and the promise are mismatched, better wording simply increases the number of people who correctly conclude that this is not for them.
sparks.apply: Write one paragraph describing the person you serve without using demographics, focusing entirely on what they want and what they currently do instead.

sparks.hook: Pick the smallest audience you could possibly succeed with.
sparks.insight: The instinct is to widen: more segments, more use cases, a bigger addressable market. Widening makes the promise vaguer, and a vague promise is easy to ignore. Starting narrow does the opposite — it lets you make a specific claim, build exactly the right thing, and be genuinely the best option for a group small enough to actually reach. Growth from there is a choice you make later, from a position where some people already care, rather than a hope you start with.
sparks.why: This is contested. Byron Sharp's work at the Ehrenberg-Bass Institute argues most brand growth comes from broad reach and light buyers, not deep niche loyalty. Read the narrow start as advice for the early, resource-poor stage.
sparks.apply: Define the smallest group for whom your product would be the obvious first choice, then remove one feature that exists only to appeal to somebody else.

carousel.title: Describe one person
carousel.body: Write a single real customer, not a segment: their situation, what they have already tried, what they say when it goes wrong. Segments are averages, and nobody is an average.

carousel.title: Cut until it hurts
carousel.body: Remove every group you are including out of hope rather than evidence. What remains should be small enough that you could plausibly reach most of them.

carousel.title: Make an obvious promise
carousel.body: State what changes for that group in one sentence with no hedging. If the sentence would suit a competitor equally well, it is still far too broad.

carousel.title: Earn the right to widen
carousel.body: Only expand once the first group buys, returns and refers. Broadening before that hides the fact that nobody was actually convinced yet.

sparks.hook: People do not buy what you make. They buy who it lets them become.
sparks.insight: Nobody wants the drill, the software licence or the course. They want the state on the other side: the shelf up, the team calm, the feeling of being someone who has that handled. Underneath most purchases sits a small identity claim — the kind of person who buys this. If you can name the change your customer is trying to make in their own life, and how it will look to the people around them, you can build and describe the product far more precisely than any feature list allows.
sparks.why: This restates a long-standing idea in marketing: customers hire a product for the change it produces. It holds up because features get compared while outcomes get chosen, and only one of those is a decision.
sparks.apply: Write the sentence a customer would say about themselves after using your product for six months. Then check that the product actually delivers it.

sparks.hook: Trust is built by showing up repeatedly, not by being clever once.
sparks.insight: A single brilliant campaign buys attention that evaporates. What compounds is consistency: publishing on a schedule, keeping small promises, sounding like the same organisation every time. This is slow and it looks unimpressive for months, which is why most people abandon it for another launch. But the people you want are wary, they have been marketed at all their lives, and the only signal that reliably separates you from the noise is the passage of time with no unpleasant surprises.
sparks.why: Repeated, predictable contact lowers perceived risk, and perceived risk is what stops most qualified buyers. The effect is cumulative and cannot be bought quickly, which is exactly why it is defensible.
sparks.apply: Commit to one publishing rhythm you could sustain in your worst week, not your best, and hold it for twelve weeks before judging whether it works.

carousel.title: Pick a sustainable pace
carousel.body: Choose the frequency you could hold during a bad month. A weekly rhythm kept for a year beats a daily one abandoned in March, because the promise is the product.

carousel.title: Say the same things
carousel.body: Consistency of position matters more than variety of topic. People need several exposures before they can describe what you stand for to somebody else.

carousel.title: Keep small promises
carousel.body: Deliver on time, answer messages, do what the page said you would. Small kept promises are the cheapest available evidence that the large ones are safe.

carousel.title: Wait longer than feels sane
carousel.body: Judge the work in quarters, not weeks. Reputation accumulates below the surface, and switching approach every month resets the clock every month.

sparks.hook: Status is doing quiet work behind most purchases you make.
sparks.insight: Every group has an internal pecking order and a set of signals about who is rising and who is not. Buying decisions ride on that more often than people admit — the tools, the brands, the choices that mark you as serious, or thrifty, or ahead. This is not vanity; it is how humans navigate groups. If you can see what counts as status among the people you serve, and whether they want to climb or simply to belong, you can build something that fits rather than something that quietly embarrasses them.
sparks.why: Status-seeking is well documented across social psychology and consumer research. It is uncomfortable to write into a marketing plan, which is why competitors usually leave the insight sitting on the table.
sparks.apply: Ask five customers who they compare themselves to at work. Note what they admire in those people, then check whether your product helps them look like that.

sparks.hook: Empathy means accepting that other people want things you find ridiculous.
sparks.insight: The most common marketing error is assuming customers are versions of you with less information. They are not. They have different beliefs, different constraints, different ideas about what is worth money. Real empathy is not sympathy or kindness — it is the discipline of accepting that a person can be entirely rational and still want something you would never buy. Once you stop trying to correct them, you can start building for the world as they actually see it.
sparks.why: Projection is the default setting: people estimate others' preferences by consulting their own. It is a persistent, well-documented bias, and it is fatal in a job whose whole task is predicting what someone else wants.
sparks.apply: Find one thing your customers do that irritates you, and write out the version of the story in which their behaviour is completely sensible.

sparks.hook: You cannot make someone want something. You can find people who already do.
sparks.insight: Persuasion at scale barely works. What works is search: locating the people whose existing desires point at what you are building, then making it obvious to them. That reframes the whole job. You stop trying to change minds and start trying to be found by the right ones, which means clearer positioning, sharper language and a willingness to say plainly who this is not for. Saying who it is not for is what makes the yes credible.
sparks.why: Changing a settled preference is slow and expensive; matching an existing one is fast and cheap. Most marketing budgets are spent attempting the first while calling it awareness building.
sparks.apply: Add one line to your homepage stating clearly who this is not for, and watch what it does to the quality of the enquiries you receive.

sparks.hook: Tension moves people. Manufactured anxiety just makes them close the tab.
sparks.insight: Useful marketing creates a small gap between where someone is and where they could be, and holds it open until they act. That is tension, and it is honest — the person genuinely wants the thing on the other side. Manufactured fear is different: fake scarcity, countdown timers, invented threats. It converts in the short run and costs you the only asset that compounds, which is the belief that you tell the truth. The test is whether the gap would still exist if you had never mentioned it.
sparks.why: Pressure tactics work at the margin and damage repeat purchase and referral, which is where most durable value sits. The line between tension and manipulation is whether the problem is real without you.
sparks.apply: Audit your funnel for anything urgent that is not actually true — timers, false scarcity, invented deadlines — and delete one of them this week.

sparks.hook: Your best customers were sold to by other customers, not by you.
sparks.insight: Growth that lasts is almost always transmitted person to person, which means the marketing task is to make that transmission easy. That is partly product and partly language: giving people a clear, short way to describe what you do, an obvious moment when recommending you makes sense, and a result impressive enough to be worth attaching their own name to. Nobody recommends something that might embarrass them, so reliability is itself a marketing feature.
sparks.why: A recommendation carries the recommender's credibility, so its cost to them is reputational. Products that occasionally fail generate far less word of mouth than their average quality would suggest.
sparks.apply: Write the twelve-word description you want customers to use about you, then check whether your three most recent referrals said anything close to it.

sparks.hook: If nobody would miss you, you have not really made anything yet.
sparks.insight: The clean test of whether the work matters is subtraction. If your product disappeared tomorrow, who would notice within a week, and what specifically would be worse for them? A vague answer means you have built something substitutable, and substitutable things compete on price forever. A sharp answer tells you exactly who to serve, what to protect and where to invest, because you now know the precise reason you exist to somebody.
sparks.why: Missability is a proxy for switching cost and emotional attachment at the same time. It is harder to fool yourself about than satisfaction scores, which are famously generous and weakly linked to behaviour.
sparks.apply: Ask ten customers what they would use instead if you closed tomorrow. If most name a competitor without hesitating, you have a differentiation problem.

actions: Write a one-page description of the smallest group you could serve completely, covering what they already believe and what they do instead of buying from you.
Add a plain statement of who your product is not for to your website, and track whether enquiry quality improves over the following month.
Choose a publishing rhythm you could sustain through your worst month and hold it for twelve weeks before changing anything about the approach.
Ask ten customers what they would switch to if you closed tomorrow, and use the answers to find the one thing worth being irreplaceable at.
books.not_for_you_if: You want measurable tactics, channel mechanics or media buying rather than a philosophy of audience and trust, or you need evidence more than aphorism.

verification.notes: Published 2018 by Portfolio. Its niche-first advice sits in genuine tension with mass-reach research from the Ehrenberg-Bass Institute; both views are noted in the sparks. All prose here is original.

books.title: Traction
books.subtitle: Get a Grip on Your Business
books.author: Gino Wickman
books.why_it_matters: It gave small companies a full operating routine — meetings, numbers, priorities, roles — instead of another book about vision. Thousands of firms now run some version of it. Treat it as a practitioner's system rather than researched truth: there is no independent evidence base behind the framework.

crux.headline: Rhythm beats brilliance in a small company
crux.body: A small business rarely dies of bad strategy. It dies of a hundred good intentions that never got a slot in the week. So install the plumbing: one page of direction everyone can repeat, a handful of priorities per quarter, a short sheet of weekly numbers, a meeting with a fixed shape, and one list where every problem waits its turn. Dull, repeatable machinery is what turns an owner's ideas into a company that runs without them.

sparks.hook: Your company is not short of ideas. It is short of a week that repeats.
sparks.insight: Small companies rarely fail because the founder ran out of good ideas. They fail because nothing in the calendar forces the good idea to become a shipped thing. An operating system fixes that by making a few rhythms non-negotiable: a yearly direction, a ninety-day set of priorities, a weekly meeting with a fixed shape, a short list of numbers checked every Monday. None of it is clever. Its power is that it runs whether or not anyone feels inspired, which is most weeks.
sparks.why: Founders over-index on strategy because strategy is fun and cheap. Execution is repetitive and dull, so it gets skipped first — which is exactly why a system that runs without motivation outperforms one that needs it.
sparks.apply: Block the same ninety minutes every week for a leadership meeting and do not move it for a customer, a fire or a flight. Protect the slot for a full quarter.

sparks.hook: If eight people describe the plan eight ways, you do not have a plan.
sparks.insight: A strategy that lives in the founder's head is a private hobby. The test is not whether you can explain it. It is whether every leader can state, without prompting, what the company is for, who it serves, what it refuses to do, and what has to be true in three years. Getting there means writing it on a single page and repeating it far past the point where you are bored of your own words. Boredom in the leader is roughly the point where the message starts landing with everyone else.
sparks.why: Repetition is not condescension. People hear a message intermittently, in fragments, while distracted by their own work, so the sender always hits saturation long before the audience reaches comprehension.
sparks.apply: Ask each leader separately to write the company's three-year picture in five lines, then compare the answers side by side without editing them.

sparks.hook: Two different questions: is this the right person, and is this the right seat?
sparks.insight: Hiring pain usually comes from collapsing two separate judgements into one. The first is about values: does this person behave the way the company needs, regardless of role. The second is about fit: do they understand the job, actually want it, and have the capacity to do it at the size you are becoming. A great person in the wrong seat looks like a performance problem and gets managed as one, which fixes nothing. Separate the questions and the right action becomes obvious — coach, move, or part ways.
sparks.why: Values misfits damage a team even when they perform, and seat misfits fail even when they are loved. Treating both as underperformance produces the wrong intervention about half the time.
sparks.apply: List your team on paper. Mark each person twice: values fit yes or no, and seat fit yes or no. Act only on the boxes that are honestly no.

carousel.title: Name the behaviours
carousel.body: Write the three or four behaviours the company actually rewards, drawn from your best people rather than from a poster. Vague values like integrity fail this test because nobody ever fails them.

carousel.title: Score people, not roles
carousel.body: Rate each person against those behaviours with evidence, not impressions. One recent example either way is enough. Ratings without examples turn into popularity contests.

carousel.title: Test the seat separately
carousel.body: Ask three things about the job: do they grasp it, do they want it, and can they carry it at next year's volume. A no on any one is a different problem with a different fix.

carousel.title: Choose within a quarter
carousel.body: Decide to coach, move or exit, and set a date. Leaving a known mismatch unresolved teaches everyone that the standards are decorative.

sparks.hook: A year is too long to plan and a week is too short. Ninety days is the unit.
sparks.insight: Annual goals rot quietly. By March the world has moved and nobody remembers what was agreed in January, so the year ends in a scramble. Quarterly priorities are short enough that you can still see the finish line and long enough to finish something real. The discipline is the number: three to seven for the company, and a handful each for a person. Anything longer is a wish list, because a list of fifteen priorities is a way of saying nothing is a priority while sounding organised.
sparks.why: Ninety days sits inside most people's planning horizon, so commitments stay vivid. Cutting the list creates the scarcity that forces the actual trade-off conversation, which is the part organisations avoid.
sparks.apply: Choose at most five things that must be finished this quarter, name one owner per item, and write the date each one is done by.

sparks.hook: A monthly profit report tells you about a month you can no longer influence.
sparks.insight: Financial statements are a lagging record of decisions already made. What a small company needs instead is a short weekly sheet of leading numbers — calls booked, quotes sent, jobs completed, cash collected, tickets open — each with a name and a target next to it. Five to fifteen lines, looked at every week by the same people. When a number goes off, you find out inside seven days instead of at the month-end review, and the fix is still cheap.
sparks.why: Leading measures move before the outcome does, so they buy reaction time. The weekly cadence matters as much as the metrics: monthly review means the average problem runs unchecked for a fortnight.
sparks.apply: Build a single sheet of no more than fifteen weekly numbers, each owned by one person with a target, and review it at the top of every leadership meeting.

sparks.hook: Your weekly meeting is a status update. That is why everyone hates it.
sparks.insight: Most leadership meetings spend their time on information that could have been an email, then run out of clock exactly when the hard thing surfaces. Flip the ratio. Keep reporting to a few tight minutes — numbers, priorities, headline news — and give the bulk of the hour to a ranked list of real problems, working them one at a time until they are actually resolved. Same day, same time, same shape, every week. Predictability is what lets people bring the awkward item instead of saving it.
sparks.why: A fixed agenda removes the negotiation about what the meeting is for, and the fixed slot removes the negotiation about whether it happens. Both negotiations are where good meeting habits usually die.
sparks.apply: Rewrite next week's agenda so at least half the time is reserved for solving a ranked list of problems, and cut every item that is pure reporting.

carousel.title: Start with the numbers
carousel.body: Run the weekly scorecard fast. Each owner says on track or off track, nothing more. Discussion of an off number goes to the problem list, not into the reporting section.

carousel.title: Check the quarter
carousel.body: Each priority owner says on track or off. Again, no explanation. The point is to surface drift early, not to hold a defence hearing in front of colleagues.

carousel.title: Build the list
carousel.body: Collect every problem worth the group's time, including new ones raised in the room, then rank the top three by the cost of leaving them alone for another week.

carousel.title: Solve one at a time
carousel.body: Take the first item, agree what the real problem is, argue it once, then decide. Move to the next only when someone owns an action with a date.

carousel.title: Close with actions
carousel.body: Read back every commitment made and who owns it. A meeting that ends without a written list of owners and dates has produced conversation, not progress.

sparks.hook: Half your arguments are about the symptom, not the thing underneath it.
sparks.insight: Teams burn hours debating a surface complaint — this client is difficult, the handover is messy — while the actual problem sits one layer down and never gets named. Before anyone proposes a solution, force the group to agree in one sentence on what the problem is. It usually takes several attempts and it feels like a delay. It is not. Once the real issue is stated plainly, the answer is often obvious and the discussion collapses from forty minutes to five.
sparks.why: Solution talk is more comfortable than problem talk because it feels productive. The cost is that a group can agree enthusiastically on a fix for something that was never the cause.
sparks.apply: Next time an argument passes ten minutes, stop and make someone state the problem in one sentence everyone accepts before any solution is allowed.

sparks.hook: Write down the annoying thing instead of discussing it right now.
sparks.insight: Most small companies have no place to put a problem, so problems get raised whenever they are felt — mid-corridor, mid-project, mid-someone-else's meeting. Keeping a single visible list changes the economics. Anything that is not on fire goes on the list and waits for the weekly slot where it can be properly argued and closed. Interruptions drop, the same complaint stops recirculating, and the list itself becomes an honest picture of what the company is avoiding.
sparks.why: A capture point separates noticing from solving. Without one, urgency sets the agenda, and urgency is a poor judge of importance in a business that is not actually on fire.
sparks.apply: Open one shared list today, name it plainly, and require that anything raised outside a genuine fire goes there first and gets worked in the weekly meeting.

sparks.hook: Design the seats your company needs, then see who fits them.
sparks.insight: The usual org chart is a map of who you happened to hire. Reverse it. Sketch the functions the business genuinely needs at the size you are heading toward, write the three to five outcomes each one owns, and only then put names in boxes. Founders find this uncomfortable because their own name lands in four boxes at once, which is precisely the diagnosis. Every function with no clear owner is a place where work quietly becomes nobody's job and shows up later as a fire.
sparks.why: Structure should follow the work, not the people, or you end up designing the company around the strengths and blind spots of whoever joined first. That constraint gets more expensive every year.
sparks.apply: Draw the structure your business needs eighteen months from now with outcomes written under each box, leave the names off, and fill them in last.

sparks.hook: You do not need a process manual. You need seven processes written thinly.
sparks.insight: Documentation projects die because people try to capture everything. The useful version is smaller: identify the handful of processes the business actually runs on — how you win work, deliver it, bill it, hire — and write only the steps that must not vary. A page each, not a binder. Then make everyone follow the same version. Consistency is what lets you hand work to a newer and less experienced person without quality collapsing, which is the only way an owner ever gets their week back.
sparks.why: Variation is where quality and margin leak. Capturing the critical few steps removes most of the variation at a fraction of the cost of full documentation, which almost nobody ever finishes anyway.
sparks.apply: Name your core processes on one page this week, then have each owner draft only the steps that must never change. Cap each at a single page.

actions: Write your company's direction on a single page, then ask every leader to reproduce it from memory a week later and fix whatever nobody could recall.
Cut next quarter's plan to five finished outcomes with one named owner and one due date each, and delete everything else from the list.
Build a fifteen-line weekly scorecard with a target and an owner per line, and start every leadership meeting by reading it in under five minutes.
Run the same meeting agenda for eight consecutive weeks before judging it, and keep a written list of every problem the company keeps postponing.
books.not_for_you_if: You run a large or highly technical organisation, or you find prescriptive branded frameworks with trademarked tool names harder to take seriously than plain advice.

verification.notes: Self-published in 2007 and widely reissued by BenBella in 2011; the framework is the Entrepreneurial Operating System. It is a practitioner framework with no independent research base. All prose here is original.

books.title: Zero to One
books.subtitle: Notes on Startups, or How to Build the Future
books.author: Peter Thiel and Blake Masters
books.why_it_matters: It is the sharpest available argument against the received wisdom that competition is healthy for the firms in it, and the clearest statement of how venture investing actually works. Whether or not you accept it, it forces you to defend your position.

crux.headline: Competition is not a badge. It is a tax
crux.body: A business in a genuinely competitive market makes no lasting profit, because rivals will keep bidding away whatever surplus appears. The businesses worth building are the ones that do something nobody else can do, and that keep doing it long enough for the returns to accumulate. So the aim is not to be a better version of an existing company but to make something new, then own the small market it creates before expanding outward.

sparks.hook: Every happy company is different. Every miserable one has competitors.
sparks.insight: Businesses that make sustained profits are doing something nobody else can do, which means each of them is unusual in its own way. Businesses stuck in fierce competition all look alike, because competition forces them to converge on the same practices and the same prices. The argument runs against how competition is normally described in business culture, where rivalry is treated as evidence of a healthy market and of your own toughness. For consumers it often is healthy. For the firms inside it, it is mostly a transfer of value to the buyer.
sparks.why: Read it as a claim about where profit accumulates, not as a policy position. Economists agree competitive markets compress producer margins; the disagreement is whether that is a problem to be solved or the point of the system.
sparks.apply: Write down what your company does that no rival could do within two years. If nothing survives that test, you are competing rather than building.

sparks.hook: What important truth do very few people agree with you about?
sparks.insight: The most useful question to ask a founder, or yourself, is where your beliefs diverge from consensus in a way you could defend. It is hard because most contrarian answers are either wrong or merely unpopular rather than genuinely unrecognised. But valuable companies are built on something true that most people have not yet accepted, since anything obvious has already been done by somebody better resourced than you. If your idea is widely agreed to be good, the returns have been competed away before you start.
sparks.why: The test filters for asymmetry of information or judgement, which is what an edge actually is. Its failure mode is rewarding contrarianism for its own sake, which produces confident nonsense rather than insight.
sparks.apply: Write one belief you hold that most people in your field reject, plus the evidence you would show them. Then ask a smart sceptic to attack it.

sparks.hook: Being first is worth little. Being last is worth everything.
sparks.insight: Moving early is often mistaken for the source of advantage, but the early mover carries the cost of educating a market and is frequently overtaken. What actually matters is generating the majority of the cash flows in your market for years after the excitement has passed. That reframes the question from how quickly you can launch to whether the business will still be dominant in a decade. Most valuations are made of distant cash flows, so a business that fades in five years is worth far less than its early growth suggests.
sparks.why: The point is that value sits in duration rather than in timing. Testing durability is hard and speculative, but asking it early prevents you from mistaking a fast start for a lasting position.
sparks.apply: Ask what your business will look like in ten years and what would have to be true for you to still lead. Write the three biggest threats to that.

sparks.hook: Four things separate a durable business from a lucky one.
sparks.insight: A position that lasts usually rests on some combination of four things: technology so much better that copying is impractical rather than merely expensive, a product that improves as more people use it, a cost structure that gets better with scale rather than worse, and a brand that buyers trust enough to pay for. One of these alone is fragile. Several together are why some businesses hold their position for decades while apparently similar rivals with more funding never establish one at all.
sparks.why: These are recognisable in most durably profitable businesses, though the framing is an argument rather than a study. Brand in particular can be a consequence of dominance rather than a cause of it.
sparks.apply: Score your business honestly on all four. If you cannot claim two of them, decide which one you will build before you spend on growth.

carousel.title: Proprietary technology
carousel.body: Not slightly better, but so much better on a dimension buyers care about that matching it would take a rival years. Marginal improvements get copied within a release cycle.

carousel.title: Network effects
carousel.body: The product gets more valuable as more people use it. These are powerful once established and brutally hard to start, since the early product is worth little to the first users.

carousel.title: Economies of scale
carousel.body: Costs per unit fall as you grow, so size itself becomes a defence. Service businesses often lack this, which is why they rarely produce durable dominance.

carousel.title: Branding
carousel.body: A name buyers trust enough to choose without comparison shopping. Real only when it rests on a genuine product difference, otherwise it is marketing spend with a short half-life.

sparks.hook: Start with a market so small that people laugh at the ambition.
sparks.insight: The instinct is to describe a huge addressable market, because a big number makes a plan look exciting. In practice a large market means a fragmented one with entrenched competitors, and a small share of it is worth very little. It is far better to dominate a tiny, specific group of users completely, because that gives you real revenue, real feedback and a defensible base. Expansion then happens outward into adjacent groups from a position of strength rather than as a scramble for scraps.
sparks.why: Dominating a niche gives you pricing power and word of mouth inside a group that talks to itself. The risk is picking a niche with no adjacent markets to expand into, which produces a comfortable business that cannot grow.
sparks.apply: Define a group of users small enough that you could serve most of them personally, and write down what winning all of them would take.

sparks.hook: One investment returns more than the entire rest of the fund.
sparks.insight: Venture returns are not spread evenly. A very small number of investments produce almost all the gains, and the rest collectively return roughly nothing. That has consequences beyond investing. It means a fund should only make bets that could plausibly be the outlier, since a moderately successful company does not move the total. It also means a founder should think hard about which company to join and which project to pursue, because effort spread across many options mostly lands in the part of the distribution that returns nothing.
sparks.why: Extreme skew in venture outcomes is well documented across funds. Applying the same logic to careers is an extension rather than a finding, and it understates how much people learn from the bets that fail.
sparks.apply: List where your time went last quarter. If it was spread across five things, pick the one that could matter most and give it half your hours.

sparks.hook: If you cannot name your distribution channel, you do not have one.
sparks.insight: Technical people systematically undervalue selling, because good selling is invisible when done well and embarrassing when done badly. But a product does not spread on merit alone, and the cost of acquiring a customer has to be lower than what that customer is worth over their lifetime, or the business does not work at whatever scale you reach. The right method depends almost entirely on deal size: an enterprise contract needs a person, a mid-sized purchase needs a repeatable sales process, and a cheap product needs distribution that costs almost nothing per user.
sparks.why: The distinction is practical and easy to check. Most failures here come from applying a sales model suited to one price point to a product priced at a completely different one.
sparks.apply: Calculate what a customer is worth over their lifetime and what you spend to get one. If the ratio is under three, fix distribution before building more product.

carousel.title: Work out the deal size
carousel.body: Average revenue per customer decides everything else about how you sell. Write it down before choosing a channel, because the channel has to be cheaper than the deal.

carousel.title: Match the method
carousel.body: Large contracts justify a person and a long cycle. Mid-sized ones need a repeatable process. Small ones need marketing or word of mouth, since no human can be involved profitably.

carousel.title: Check the arithmetic
carousel.body: Compare lifetime value against acquisition cost. A gap that only works at hypothetical future scale is not a business model, it is an argument for more funding.

carousel.title: Own one channel first
carousel.body: One channel working reliably beats five that half work. Spreading effort across channels usually means none of them reaches the volume where the economics improve.

sparks.hook: The belief that everything worth finding has been found is the mistake.
sparks.insight: There is a widespread assumption that the easy discoveries are done and the remaining questions belong to large institutions with large budgets. That assumption is convenient because it excuses not looking. Yet plenty of valuable things are unpopular to investigate, socially awkward to raise, or simply outside the areas where credentialled attention is currently pointed. The practical version is not mysticism: pick a domain, examine what everyone assumes without checking, and look specifically at the places where the assumption has never been tested.
sparks.why: Areas that are unfashionable are systematically under-searched because attention follows funding and status. That is a real structural gap, though it is also where a great deal of genuinely worthless work sits.
sparks.apply: Pick one thing everyone in your field takes for granted and spend a week trying to verify it from primary sources rather than from repetition.

sparks.hook: A plan you believe in beats optimism with no plan behind it.
sparks.insight: You can be optimistic or pessimistic about the future, and separately you can have a specific plan or none. The combination that builds things is optimism with a definite plan: the belief that the future can be better and a concrete idea of how to make it so. The dominant modern posture is optimism without a plan, which shows up as diversification, endless optionality and keeping doors open. That posture is rational for an individual managing risk and terrible for anyone trying to build something specific.
sparks.why: The distinction is a useful lens rather than a tested claim. It does explain why institutions that hedge everything struggle to produce anything, and why concentrated conviction is required for large projects.
sparks.apply: Write the specific future you are working towards and the sequence of steps to it. If you cannot, you are keeping options open rather than building.

sparks.hook: This is an argument from an investor with a stake in the conclusion.
sparks.insight: Two caveats belong with the book. It is written by a venture investor whose returns depend on the small number of firms that escape competition, so the advice to seek dominance describes what is good for that portfolio as much as what is good for the world. And the evidence is illustrative rather than systematic: memorable examples selected after the fact, without any account of the many founders who followed the same advice and failed. The reasoning is worth engaging with. The confidence exceeds what it can support.
sparks.why: The strongest objection is that concentrated market power benefits owners and often harms buyers, which the book treats as a secondary concern. Read it as a sharp partial argument rather than a balanced account.
sparks.apply: For each claim you find persuasive, ask who benefits if you believe it, then look for one counter-example before acting on it.

actions: Write down what your company does that no competitor could replicate within two years, and be honest if the list comes out empty.
Define a group of users small enough that you could serve nearly all of them, then plan what taking that whole group would require.
Calculate customer lifetime value against acquisition cost, and fix distribution before adding features if the ratio is weak.
Take the argument you found most convincing and spend an hour looking for the strongest published objection to it.
books.not_for_you_if: You want systematic evidence rather than argument, or you are uncomfortable taking strategic advice framed around building market power.

verification.notes: Published 2014 by Crown Business, developed from Blake Masters's notes on a Stanford course taught by Thiel in 2012. The argument is polemical and its examples are chosen retrospectively. All prose here is original.

books.title: $100M Offers
books.subtitle: How to Make Offers So Good People Feel Stupid Saying No
books.author: Alex Hormozi
books.why_it_matters: A blunt, unusually specific treatment of the thing most founders leave vague: what exactly you are selling and why anyone should pay a premium for it. It reset how a generation of small service businesses package and price their work.

crux.headline: Build an offer nobody can price-compare
crux.body: If a customer can line you up beside three alternatives, the cheapest one wins and your margin disappears. The escape is to construct an offer specific enough that no direct comparison exists: a defined outcome for a defined person, with the obstacles between them and that outcome removed, the risk shifted onto you, and a price set by the value of the result rather than by what competitors charge.

sparks.hook: If customers can compare you like for like, you have already lost.
sparks.insight: Selling something that looks like everyone else's version forces the conversation onto price, and there is always somebody willing to go lower. The way out is not better salesmanship but a different offer: aimed at a narrower customer, promising a specific result rather than a service category, and bundled so that no competitor's package maps onto yours. When there is nothing directly comparable, the customer has to evaluate the outcome instead of the rate, and that is a conversation you can win.
sparks.why: Price competition is a consequence of substitutability. Reduce how substitutable you look and you change what the buyer is actually weighing up, without changing what you deliver.
sparks.apply: Rewrite your main offer to name one specific customer and one specific result, and remove every phrase a competitor could also honestly use.

sparks.hook: Choose the hungry market first. A great offer cannot rescue a bad one.
sparks.insight: The most carefully built offer will fail if it is pointed at people who do not urgently want the outcome or cannot pay for it. Market choice comes first and it dominates everything after. Look for people in real pain about this problem, with money to spend, who can be reached as a group, in a category that is growing rather than shrinking. Get those four right and a mediocre offer still sells. Get them wrong and no amount of packaging will rescue the business.
sparks.why: Demand is a property of the market, not of your marketing. Persuasion can shift which supplier a motivated buyer chooses; it cannot manufacture urgency in people who do not have the problem.
sparks.apply: Score your current market on pain, purchasing power, reachability and growth. If any score is low, fix the market before touching the offer.

carousel.title: Find real pain
carousel.body: Look for a problem people already lose sleep, money or status over. Mild inconvenience does not produce buyers, however elegantly you describe the solution.

carousel.title: Check they can pay
carousel.body: Confirm the buyer has budget and the authority to spend it. Serving people who genuinely need you and cannot afford you is charity with a pricing page.

carousel.title: Check you can reach them
carousel.body: Ask how you would put a message in front of a thousand of these people next month. A group with no gathering place is expensive to sell to for ever.

carousel.title: Check the direction
carousel.body: Prefer a market growing for structural reasons. Rising demand forgives ordinary execution; a shrinking market punishes even very good work.

sparks.hook: Four levers set perceived value, and only one of them is the result.
sparks.insight: What a buyer feels an offer is worth rises with the outcome they want and how likely they think you are to deliver it. It falls with how long they will wait and how much effort or sacrifice it demands from them. Most sellers push only on the first lever by promising bigger results. The other three are usually easier to move and far more credible: prove the likelihood with evidence, shorten the time to a first visible win, and take work off the customer's plate.
sparks.why: The framework is a practitioner heuristic rather than a measured model, but it directs attention usefully, because effort and delay are the objections buyers raise most and sellers address least.
sparks.apply: Take your offer and improve one lever other than the promise: cut the time to first result, or remove one thing the customer has to do.

carousel.title: Sharpen the outcome
carousel.body: State the result in the customer's own terms and make it concrete. A vague benefit cannot be valued, so buyers default to comparing your price instead.

carousel.title: Raise believability
carousel.body: Show evidence that it works: case detail, references, a trial, a guarantee. Most buyers doubt the likelihood far more than they doubt the value.

carousel.title: Shorten the wait
carousel.body: Engineer a visible win in the first days rather than the first quarter. Delayed payoff reduces perceived value and increases the chance of cancellation.

carousel.title: Remove the effort
carousel.body: Every task you hand back to the customer lowers what your offer is worth. Do it for them wherever the cost to you is less than the value they place on it.

sparks.hook: Charging more can improve the results your customers get.
sparks.insight: A higher price changes who buys and how they behave after buying. People who pay seriously turn up, do the work and take the advice, and consequently get better outcomes, which produces better testimonials and more referrals. A low price attracts buyers who are least committed and most demanding, which is a miserable combination. Raising prices also funds a better product. The obvious caveat is that this only holds if you can genuinely deliver at the higher price.
sparks.why: Higher commitment correlates with follow-through, which is the mechanism behind the effect. It is not magic, and a premium price attached to a weak service produces refunds and reputational damage quickly.
sparks.apply: Raise the price of your main offer for the next five prospects only, and record the conversion rate and the quality of clients you get.

sparks.hook: Never discount. Add something instead.
sparks.insight: Cutting price to close a deal teaches the buyer that your first number was not real and sets the anchor for every renewal. Adding something of value keeps the price intact and gives the customer more reason to say yes. The addition should cost you far less than it is worth to them, which is why templates, extra access, a faster start or an extended guarantee work well. You are moving the perceived value up rather than the price down, and only one of those is reversible.
sparks.why: Discounts anchor future expectations and signal that the price was arbitrary. Additions preserve the anchor and are far easier to withdraw later without a confrontation.
sparks.apply: Prepare three additions you can offer instead of a discount, each costing you little and clearly worth something to the buyer.

sparks.hook: List everything standing between the customer and the result, then remove it.
