Fishkin eventually stepped out of the chief executive role and writes plainly about how long he stayed past the point where he knew. Self-awareness about which job you are good at is worth more than the resolve to endure the wrong one.
sparks.why: Founder and chief executive are conflated by convention and by ego, not by evidence. The skills correlate weakly, and the cost of the mismatch is paid by everyone in the company.
sparks.apply: Write out the parts of your role you dread, and ask whether they are temporary discomfort or a permanent mismatch with what you are good at.

sparks.hook: Your health is a company asset and you are depreciating it fast.
sparks.insight: Fishkin describes a stretch of severe depression while running the company, and is direct that the culture around him treated exhaustion as evidence of commitment. The arithmetic is simple and mostly ignored: a founder who cannot think clearly makes worse decisions, and in a small company decisions are the entire output. Sleep, treatment and time away are not rewards for hitting a target. They are inputs to the only asset the business genuinely cannot replace at short notice.
sparks.why: Sleep loss measurably degrades judgement and risk assessment. In a company where a handful of people make every consequential call, that degradation is a direct operating cost rather than a personal matter.
sparks.apply: Book the medical or therapeutic appointment you have deferred, this week, and put a recurring non-negotiable stop time in your calendar.

sparks.hook: A funding announcement is marketing, not a scoreboard.
sparks.insight: A rival raising a large round tells you that some investors made a bet, and nothing about whether the business works. The number is chosen partly for the press, the valuation reflects terms nobody publishes, and the announcement is timed for recruiting and sales rather than accuracy. Founders read these as evidence they are losing and reshape strategy in response. The only comparisons worth acting on are the ones you can verify: retention, revenue, and whether customers switch.
sparks.why: Announcements are a controlled disclosure by a party with an interest in appearing strong. Treating them as information about business quality is reading a company's own advertising as an audit.
sparks.apply: The next time a competitor announces a round, write down what it actually tells you about their customers. Then get back to your own retention numbers.

actions: Model your own equity at three exit prices, including a mediocre one, using the actual preference terms in your signed documents rather than the headline valuation.
Write down the outcome that would genuinely make you happy in seven years, then check whether your current funding structure can accommodate it.
Choose one number you have kept vague with your team and publish it internally along with your plan for it.
Book the health appointment you have been deferring and set a recurring weekly stop time that you defend as firmly as a customer meeting.
books.not_for_you_if: You want a tactical playbook with frameworks and checklists. This is a personal account whose value is in its honesty, not in a reusable system.

verification.notes: Published 2018 by Portfolio. Fishkin co-founded Moz and later SparkToro. Prose here is original; no wording reproduced.

books.title: Profit First
books.subtitle: Transform Your Business from a Cash-Eating Monster to a Money-Making Machine
books.author: Mike Michalowicz
books.why_it_matters: It took a behavioural insight that accountants had ignored — owners manage from their bank balance, not their accounts — and turned it into a cash system that thousands of small businesses actually stuck with.

crux.headline: Take your profit first and run the business on what is left
crux.body: The conventional formula treats profit as whatever survives after expenses, which in practice means nothing survives. Reverse it. When money arrives, move a fixed share into a profit account you do not touch, along with tax and your own pay, and operate on the remainder. Constraining the operating balance forces the cost decisions you would otherwise defer indefinitely, because you can only spend what you can see.

sparks.hook: Profit is not a leftover. Take it out before you spend anything.
sparks.insight: The standard formula says revenue minus expenses equals profit, which quietly makes profit the last thing considered and the first thing sacrificed. Reverse the order. The moment money arrives, move an agreed share into an account earmarked as profit and treat the rest as everything the business has to live on. Nothing about the business changed except what you can see, and that turns out to be the part that governs your spending. You will find the costs to cut, because you have to.
sparks.why: Expenses expand to consume whatever is available, an observation that holds well for household and business spending alike. Removing money from view before you plan is the reliable countermeasure.
sparks.apply: Open a separate profit account today and move one percent of every payment into it. Do not adjust anything else for a month.

sparks.hook: Owners run their businesses off the bank balance, so use the balance.
sparks.insight: Very few small business owners read a profit and loss statement before deciding whether they can afford something. They check the bank balance. Accountants find this exasperating and it is not going to change, so the practical move is to design around the behaviour instead of against it. If the balance is the instrument people actually read, split the money across accounts so that the balance you look at every day tells you the truth about what you can spend.
sparks.why: Systems that require a behaviour change fail more often than systems that redirect the behaviour people already have. This one succeeds mainly because it demands no new financial literacy.
sparks.apply: Set your operating account as the default view in your banking app, and move every other account out of that first screen.

sparks.hook: Five accounts turn an abstract budget into a physical constraint.
sparks.insight: The mechanism is a small set of bank accounts with defined jobs. Everything lands in one account and is then distributed: a share for profit, a share for the tax you will owe, a share for paying yourself properly, and whatever remains for running the business. It looks like envelope budgeting because it is, and that is the point. A budget in a spreadsheet is a suggestion, while a budget enforced by which account holds the money is a constraint you cannot argue with at four in the afternoon.
sparks.why: Physical separation removes the decision from the moment of temptation. That is the same mechanism that makes automatic pension contributions work far better than the intention to save.
sparks.apply: Open the accounts this week and set your first allocation percentages low enough that the business survives without any changes.

carousel.title: Collect in one account
carousel.body: Every payment lands in a single income account that you never spend from. Its only job is to be the place where allocations get calculated twice a month.

carousel.title: Take profit and tax first
carousel.body: Move the profit share and the tax share out immediately, into accounts you have made deliberately awkward to reach. Tax money was never yours to spend.

carousel.title: Pay yourself properly
carousel.body: Move an owner's pay allocation next. A business that only survives by underpaying its owner is not profitable, it is subsidised by you.

carousel.title: Operate on what remains
carousel.body: Whatever is left runs the company. When it is tight, you cut costs or raise prices, which are exactly the decisions the old formula let you postpone.

carousel.title: Distribute every quarter
carousel.body: Take a real distribution from the profit account each quarter. Profit you never receive is a number on a screen and will not change how you behave.

sparks.hook: Start at one percent, because the point is the habit forming.
sparks.insight: Owners who try to start with an ambitious profit allocation usually break the business, panic and abandon the system within two months. Beginning at a share small enough that nothing has to change makes the practice survivable, and the practice is what you are actually installing. Raise the percentage by a small step each quarter and let the business adapt each time. The discipline arrives from repetition rather than from a single dramatic decision that impresses you and then collapses.
sparks.why: Behaviour change that requires no immediate sacrifice survives the first difficult month, which is when nearly all financial resolutions die. The amount matters far less than the fact that it happens every time.
sparks.apply: Set your profit allocation at one percent now and add one percentage point at the start of each quarter for the next two years.

sparks.hook: Do your money on two fixed days and never think about it in between.
sparks.insight: Allocating money whenever you happen to remember means you allocate it whenever the balance looks reassuring, which is the worst possible rule. Fixing two days a month for all transfers, supplier payments and financial review removes the daily judgement calls entirely. It also gives you a real view of your rhythm, because you see a fortnight's activity at once rather than reacting to individual payments. The rest of the month you are free to do the work that generates the money.
sparks.why: Recurring decisions consume attention and get made worse by mood and recent events. Batching them onto fixed dates converts a stream of small judgements into two considered ones.
sparks.apply: Put two recurring appointments in your calendar for money admin, on the same dates every month, and refuse to move payments between them.

sparks.hook: Put the profit account where reaching it is genuinely inconvenient.
sparks.insight: Money you can move in three taps is money you will move. Keeping the profit and tax accounts at a different bank, with no card attached and ideally with a second signature needed, is not theatre. It converts a moment of weakness into a two-day process, and almost every impulse to raid the profit account dies inside those two days. The system works because of friction rather than willpower, which is fortunate, because willpower is at its lowest exactly when cash is tight.
sparks.why: Delay between impulse and action reduces the action, a robust finding across saving, spending and consumption habits. Friction is doing the work here, not resolve.
sparks.apply: Move your profit and tax accounts to a different bank this month, remove any card, and add a second approver if you have a partner.

sparks.hook: A tight operating account is a feature. It makes you cut the right things.
sparks.insight: When the money available for running the business shrinks, you discover which costs were genuinely load-bearing. Most owners find subscriptions nobody uses, a supplier who has quietly raised prices for years, and services that were bought during an optimistic quarter. The constraint does the auditing that you have been meaning to do since last spring. Businesses reliably adapt to a smaller operating budget without customers noticing, which tells you how much of the previous spending was doing nothing at all.
sparks.why: Scarcity focuses attention on what matters, which is why the constraint works. The genuine risk is cutting investment in growth alongside the waste, and that requires judgement the system does not supply.
sparks.apply: List every recurring payment your business makes and cancel the three you would not sign up for again today.

carousel.title: List every outgoing
carousel.body: Export twelve months of transactions and write down every recurring payment. Most owners find several they had entirely forgotten they were still making.

carousel.title: Cancel the obvious
carousel.body: Remove anything you would not sign up for again today. If you are unsure whether it is used, cancelling is the cheapest way to find out.

carousel.title: Renegotiate the largest three
carousel.body: Your biggest suppliers expect to be asked and rarely are. A single conversation about rate or terms usually beats a month of small economies.

carousel.title: Protect one investment line
carousel.body: Ring-fence the spending that genuinely produces future revenue before you cut. A constraint that eats your growth budget improves this quarter and damages next year.

sparks.hook: Revenue is the number you brag about. Profit is the one you keep.
sparks.insight: Growing revenue while margins stay thin makes every problem larger: more customers to serve, more staff to manage, more working capital tied up, and no more money in your pocket. Owners chase the top line because it is visible and socially rewarding, and because a bigger business feels like a safer one. Often the opposite is true. A smaller business that keeps a healthy share of what it earns is more resilient than a larger one that keeps almost nothing.
sparks.why: Scale multiplies whatever your unit economics already are. If each sale earns you little, more sales mainly add operational risk and complexity while the owner's position stays the same.
sparks.apply: Calculate your profit per customer, then identify the customers or products below that line and either reprice them or stop serving them.

sparks.hook: Paying yourself last is not a virtue. It is a hidden subsidy.
sparks.insight: A large number of owners take whatever is left over, which is often less than they would earn as an employee doing the same work elsewhere. That is a real cost the business is not being charged for, and it hides the fact that the model does not work. Allocating your own pay before operating expenses forces the true picture into view. If the company cannot cover a market wage for the person running it, that is information about the business, not a temporary sacrifice you can absorb indefinitely.
sparks.why: Unpaid founder labour is an off-books expense. Leaving it out makes an unprofitable business look viable for years, which is how owners end up trapped in something they cannot afford to keep or leave.
sparks.apply: Write down what your role would pay elsewhere, allocate that from every payment received, and see what the business looks like afterwards.

sparks.hook: This is behaviour design, not accounting. Do not confuse the two.
sparks.insight: The system changes when you see money and how it feels to spend, and it does not change what your business actually earns. Accountants object to it for fair reasons: cash in accounts is not profit, it obscures the accrual picture, and a rigid allocation can starve a genuinely growing company of the investment it needs. Run it as a spending discipline sitting on top of real bookkeeping. If your underlying model is broken, moving money between accounts will make that obvious but will not fix it.
sparks.why: The evidence for it is practitioner experience rather than research, and the target percentages are rules of thumb rather than findings. The mechanism it borrows from behavioural economics is nonetheless well supported.
sparks.apply: Keep proper accounts alongside the system and review both with an accountant twice a year, adjusting allocations if you are underinvesting.

actions: Open separate profit, tax and owner's pay accounts this week, with the profit and tax accounts held at a different bank and no card attached.
Set your first profit allocation at one percent, schedule two fixed transfer days a month, and increase the percentage by one point each quarter.
List every recurring payment the business makes and cancel the three you would not choose to start today.
Calculate your profit per customer or per product, and either reprice or retire everything sitting below the line.
books.not_for_you_if: You run a venture-funded company burning capital by design, or you already have a finance function and disciplined accrual reporting you actually read.

verification.notes: First self-published 2014, expanded edition 2017 by Portfolio. The method is a behavioural cash system, not an accounting standard. Prose original.

books.title: Small Giants
books.subtitle: Companies That Choose to Be Great Instead of Big
books.author: Bo Burlingham
books.why_it_matters: It documented a category nobody was writing about: privately held companies that deliberately refused to grow and became remarkable instead. It gave a generation of owners permission to define success on their own terms.

crux.headline: Growth is a choice, and refusing it takes more nerve
crux.body: Every company profiled here could have expanded and decided not to, because expansion would have cost the things that made the business worth owning: control, closeness to customers, quality, a life. Refusing growth is not passive. It requires an ownership structure that permits it, an owner who actively wants it, and the discipline to turn down opportunities that any spreadsheet would tell you to take.

sparks.hook: Turning down growth was the hardest decision each of these owners made.
sparks.insight: Every one of these companies faced a moment where expanding was obviously available: a chain could open branches, a brewery could scale nationally, a manufacturer could take the contract that would triple its size. Each said no, and none found it comfortable. The pressure to grow does not come only from investors. It comes from staff wanting advancement, from suppliers, from peers, and from a culture that treats a business staying the same size as a business quietly failing.
sparks.why: Growth is the default assumption, so declining it requires an active decision repeated many times, while accepting it requires only drifting. Defaults win unless somebody deliberately resists them.
sparks.apply: Write down the last growth opportunity you accepted and list what it cost you in time, quality and control. Do the arithmetic you skipped then.

carousel.title: Price the whole cost
carousel.body: Write what the opportunity takes as well as what it pays: your hours, borrowed money, new management layers, and the quality you can no longer personally check.

carousel.title: Ask who it actually serves
carousel.body: Some expansion serves customers and some serves an idea of what a proper company looks like. Be specific about which one you are being paid in.

carousel.title: Test how reversible it is
carousel.body: A lease, a loan and a headcount jump are commitments you cannot unwind next year. Reversible bets deserve a yes far more readily than permanent ones.

carousel.title: Decide who you become
carousel.body: Describe your working week after the growth in concrete detail. If you would not choose that week on its own merits, the revenue does not change the answer.

sparks.hook: Anchor Brewing stayed small on purpose and became the reference point.
sparks.insight: Fritz Maytag took over a failing brewery and could have chased volume like every other producer. He built instead for quality and stayed deliberately small, and the result was that an entire generation of American brewers took their standards from what he did. Being the best in a narrow space is a durable position, because it is defended by craft and reputation rather than by price or scale. Bigger competitors can outspend you but cannot easily become better than you at one specific thing.
sparks.why: Reputation for excellence compounds slowly and does not transfer with an acquisition. That makes it one of the few advantages a small company can hold against a much larger one for decades.
sparks.apply: Name the one thing your business could plausibly be the best at within fifty miles, and move your next three decisions toward it.

sparks.hook: Who owns your company decides whether you are allowed to stay small.
sparks.insight: None of these businesses could have made their choices with outside investors demanding growth. Ownership structure is the mechanism, not the philosophy. Closely held shares, no venture capital, conservative debt and clear agreements among the owners are what convert a preference for staying small into an actual right to do it. Founders who intend to build this kind of company and then take money on standard growth terms discover that their intentions were never the binding part of the arrangement.
sparks.why: Capital carries obligations regardless of anyone's good intentions. Whoever can force a sale or a strategy change ultimately decides how large the company becomes, no matter what was said at the start.
sparks.apply: Read your shareholder agreement and identify who could force a sale or a growth strategy. If that person is not you, decide whether you accept that.

carousel.title: Keep control concentrated
carousel.body: Decide early how much of the company you must hold to protect its direction, and treat that threshold as a constraint on every funding conversation you have.

carousel.title: Choose patient money
carousel.body: If you need capital, prefer sources with no fixed exit horizon: retained profit, a bank facility, or investors who explicitly do not require a sale.

carousel.title: Write the intent into the documents
carousel.body: Put your position on growth, dividends and sale into the shareholder agreement. A shared understanding that lives only in conversation is worth nothing during a dispute.

carousel.title: Plan the handover early
carousel.body: Decide who inherits control and on what terms. Most companies of this kind are lost at succession, when ownership passes to people who never chose the constraint.

sparks.hook: These companies belong to a place rather than merely sitting in one.
sparks.insight: A striking common feature is deep local rootedness. Zingerman's answered demand for expansion by building more businesses in the same town rather than opening branches in other cities, keeping the founders close enough to run them properly. Being genuinely part of a community gives you suppliers who will help in a crisis, staff who stay, and customers who feel some ownership of your success. It is an advantage that a national competitor with a local branch cannot buy at any price.
sparks.why: Local reputation is built through repeated dealings with people who talk to each other. That density of relationship is what makes it costly to acquire and hard for an outsider to imitate.
sparks.apply: Pick one local relationship you have treated as transactional, and invest in it this quarter with no expectation of a return.

sparks.hook: Staying small keeps the owner in the room with the customer.
sparks.insight: The advantage these companies protect most fiercely is closeness. The owner still knows the significant customers personally, still hears the complaints directly and still notices when the quality slips. Growth breaks that link first. It gets replaced with reports, surveys and account managers, all of which are lossy translations of what one conversation would have told you. Once a founder has to read about their own customers, the speed and accuracy of every decision they make drops.
sparks.why: Direct contact carries information that surveys and dashboards strip out: tone, hesitation, the complaint the customer would not commit to a form. That information is what makes a small company adaptable.
sparks.apply: Book three customer conversations for yourself this month with no agenda and no salesperson present, and take your own notes.

sparks.hook: Generous workplaces here are demanding ones, not comfortable ones.
sparks.insight: The companies profiled treat their staff unusually well, and none of them are soft places to work. Standards are high, poor performance is addressed, and the care shows up in stability, training, honesty about the numbers and a genuine interest in what people want from their lives. Confusing generosity with lenience produces a pleasant company that slowly gets worse. The combination that actually works is a high bar plus visible commitment to the people expected to clear it.
sparks.why: People invest in work when they believe both that the standard is real and that the organisation is invested in them. Either one alone produces cynicism, in one direction or the other.
sparks.apply: Identify the performance conversation you have been avoiding and hold it this week, opening with what you are committing to do for that person.

sparks.hook: Know which business you are actually in before you optimise it.
sparks.insight: A restaurant that believes it is in the food business optimises the menu. One that understands it is in the hospitality business optimises how people feel when they arrive. A record label that thinks it sells discs behaves differently from one that thinks it protects an artist's independence. The definition determines what you measure, who you hire and what you refuse. Getting it wrong is expensive and invisible, because everything you do afterwards is competent work aimed at slightly the wrong target.
sparks.why: Business definition sets the metric, and the metric silently reorganises the company. A wrong definition rarely announces itself; it simply produces steady effort in a direction customers do not care much about.
sparks.apply: Write one sentence defining what your customers actually buy from you, then check whether your top three metrics measure that thing.

sparks.hook: Clif Bar's founder walked away from a signed sale at the last moment.
sparks.insight: Gary Erickson had a sale agreed and the paperwork ready, and he decided he did not want to hand over the company he had built. Taking the money would have been rational by every conventional measure, and he would have spent the rest of his life not running the thing he cared about. That is the trade a sale actually is. The number is the visible part; what you are selling is your own daily work and every decision about the company's future.
sparks.why: Sale decisions get made on financial models that price the business but not the seller's remaining working life. Founders who regret selling almost always describe losing the work rather than mispricing the deal.
sparks.apply: Before entertaining an offer, write down in detail what you would actually do for the next five years afterwards. Read it before you negotiate.

sparks.hook: The company stays remarkable only while somebody actively wants it to.
sparks.insight: Every business here depends on an owner who keeps choosing the constraint. That is a real vulnerability. When the founder tires, sells or dies, the successor inherits the company but not the conviction that produced it, and the default pull toward growth resumes immediately. If you build this kind of business, succession is not an administrative task for later. It is the central design problem, because a set of choices held in one person's head does not survive them.
sparks.why: Culture maintained by a single individual's judgement has no independent existence. Passing on ownership without passing on the reasoning leaves a structure that will be optimised by whoever comes next.
sparks.apply: Write down the three growth opportunities you have refused and exactly why, and give that document to whoever would run this after you.

sparks.hook: Fourteen admired companies, chosen after they were already admired.
sparks.insight: The book selects businesses that were thriving at the time of writing and looks for what they share, which is the same method that makes most business books unreliable. Plenty of companies stayed deliberately small and simply struggled. Several of these later grew, sold or ran into trouble. What survives the scepticism is narrower but genuinely useful: staying small is an available strategy, it requires specific ownership arrangements, and it works best where you can charge a premium for being distinctly better.
sparks.why: Choosing cases on the outcome cannot establish cause. The honest reading is that these are existence proofs that the choice can work, not evidence that the choice reliably works.
sparks.apply: Check whether your margins could support staying small. Without pricing power, refusing growth means refusing the only route to a viable business.

actions: Read your shareholder and loan agreements and write down exactly who has the power to force a sale or a growth strategy on your business.
Write one sentence defining what customers really buy from you, then check whether the three numbers you watch most closely actually measure it.
Book three unstructured customer conversations for yourself this month, take your own notes, and share one uncomfortable finding with your team.
Document the growth opportunities you have declined and your reasons, and hand that record to whoever might one day run the company.
books.not_for_you_if: You are building a venture-backed company aiming at a large exit. The choices described here are structurally unavailable to you once you take that money.

verification.notes: Published 2005 by Portfolio; a revised edition followed. Companies were selected while thriving, so the sample is chosen on outcome. Prose original.

books.title: Super Founders
books.subtitle: What Data Reveals About Billion-Dollar Startups
books.author: Ali Tamaseb
books.why_it_matters: Someone finally went and gathered the data instead of retelling the folklore. Tamaseb compared hundreds of billion-dollar companies against a randomly drawn comparison group, and most of what the industry believes about founders did not survive.

crux.headline: Almost everything you believe about founders is folklore
crux.body: The picture of the young technical dropout, first to market with a novel idea and a co-founder from college, is drawn from a handful of famous cases. Compared against a control group, most of those traits fail to separate the companies that reached enormous scale from the ones that did not. What did stand out was prior experience of building something significant, and entering a market big enough to matter. Use the finding to stop disqualifying yourself.

sparks.hook: Compare winners against a control group and the folklore collapses.
sparks.insight: Almost all startup wisdom is drawn from famous companies only, which cannot tell you anything. If ninety percent of enormous successes had a particular trait, but ninety percent of failures had it too, the trait is worthless as a signal. Tamaseb built a dataset of billion-dollar companies alongside a randomly selected comparison group of startups that raised money and did not get there, then checked which characteristics actually differed. Most of the celebrated ones did not.
sparks.why: This is the base-rate problem in plain form. Any claim about what winners have in common is empty until somebody checks whether the losers have it in common too.
sparks.apply: Next time you hear a rule about what successful founders do, ask what proportion of failed founders also did it. If nobody checked, discount the rule.

sparks.hook: The billion-dollar founder is usually not in their twenties.
sparks.insight: The dropout-in-a-dorm image is drawn from a handful of unusually famous cases, and it does not describe the distribution. Founders of companies that reached extreme scale skew considerably older than the myth, with a great many starting in their thirties and forties, and older founders are not rarer among the biggest outcomes. Age brings the things that actually help: knowing an industry, knowing which problems are real, and having people who will take your call.
sparks.why: Independent work on entrepreneurial age using tax and census records has pointed the same way, finding that older founders are at least as likely to build fast-growing companies. Two different methods agreeing is worth something.
sparks.apply: If you have been treating your age as a reason not to start, replace that with an inventory of the industry knowledge and contacts you already hold.

sparks.hook: The strongest signal is having built something significant before.
sparks.insight: Across the comparisons, one attribute stood out more than the usual candidates: founders who had previously built something of real consequence, whether a company that reached meaningful scale, a widely used product, or an outstanding record inside a serious organisation. Not merely having founded something before, and certainly not having attended the right school. The pattern points to demonstrated capacity to make a difficult thing exist, which is far rarer than either credentials or enthusiasm.
sparks.why: A track record is an observed sample of your actual output rather than a proxy for it. Note that this is a correlation in one hand-built dataset, and prior success also buys access to capital and talent that others cannot get.
sparks.apply: If you have not built anything at scale yet, pick a project small enough to finish this year and large enough that finishing it proves something.

sparks.hook: You do not need a co-founder, and you do not need to be technical.
sparks.insight: Two rules of thumb are handed out constantly: find a co-founder, and make sure someone on the founding team can build the product. Neither separated the huge outcomes from the rest. Solo founders are well represented among companies that reached enormous scale, and so are teams where nobody wrote code. What matters is whether the specific business needs deep technical work, and whether you can attract people who supply what you lack. The general rule is not a rule.
sparks.why: The advice is really about coverage of critical skills, which many teams achieve by hiring rather than by co-founding. Turning it into a screening rule mostly filters on convention.
sparks.apply: List the three capabilities your business genuinely requires in its first year, then decide whether each is best covered by a founder, a hire or a contract.

sparks.hook: Competitors in your market are a good sign, not a warning.
sparks.insight: Founders panic when they find rivals and take comfort in an empty field. The data suggests the opposite reading. Companies that reached extreme scale frequently entered markets that already had competitors, sometimes many, and often arrived years after the first entrants. An empty market usually means no demand has been proven, whereas a crowded one means customers exist and are already paying somebody. The question is not whether rivals exist but whether the incumbents are actually good.
sparks.why: Competition is evidence of a market. The genuine risk is not rivalry but choosing a problem nobody is willing to pay to solve, which is invisible precisely because there is nobody to look at.
sparks.apply: Map the three closest competitors and interview five of their customers about what still annoys them. Treat a crowded field as validation to exploit.

sparks.hook: First-mover advantage is mostly a story told afterwards.
sparks.insight: Being early is celebrated because the winners of any market look, in retrospect, as if they had a head start. Many companies that reached the largest outcomes were not first at all. They arrived once the market had been proven by somebody else, learned from that company's mistakes, and executed better. Being first means paying for customer education and building on immature technology. Being second or fifth means somebody else absorbed those costs on your behalf.
sparks.why: Order of entry predicts far less than execution quality and timing of the underlying technology. Pioneers frequently spend their capital proving a market that a later entrant then wins.
sparks.apply: Stop treating a competitor's launch as a lost race. Write down the three things they are doing badly and make one of those your entire pitch.

sparks.hook: Four credentials the industry worships and the data barely notices.
sparks.insight: A cluster of things founders chase turn out to be weak separators between the enormous outcomes and everyone else. Elite university names, accelerator participation, patents held, and having a novel idea nobody has had before all appear on both sides of the comparison. They are not useless, and some open doors that matter. But treating them as prerequisites means declining to start until you have collected tokens that do not predict the thing you want.
sparks.why: These attributes are highly visible, which is why they get overweighted. Visibility and predictive power are different properties, and the first is what shapes how a community talks.
sparks.apply: Write down what you are waiting to acquire before starting. For each item, ask what evidence exists that it predicts anything, then start anyway.

carousel.title: Pedigree is weakly predictive
carousel.body: Elite degrees show up among huge successes and among ordinary startups alike. They help with access to investors, which is not the same as helping the company work.

carousel.title: Accelerators are not a filter
carousel.body: Programmes give structure, contacts and a deadline, all genuinely useful. Getting in is not evidence about the outcome, and being rejected is not evidence either.

carousel.title: Patents rarely decide it
carousel.body: Outside a few sectors such as pharmaceuticals, patents seldom separate the enormous outcomes from the rest. Distribution and execution usually decide who wins.

carousel.title: Novelty is overrated
carousel.body: Plenty of the largest companies did something already being done. Many also changed their idea substantially, so the original concept was not the asset anyway.

sparks.hook: The idea is negotiable. The size of the market is not.
sparks.insight: A great many companies that reached the largest outcomes ended up selling something meaningfully different from what they started with, which tells you the initial idea was rarely the decisive asset. What is much harder to change is the market you chose to enter. A brilliant execution inside a small market produces a small company, and a mediocre execution inside an enormous one can still produce a large one. Choose the pond deliberately, because you will keep changing the fish.
sparks.why: Product direction is cheap to alter and market position is not, since it determines your customers, your channels and your ceiling. Pivots within a market are common; pivots between markets usually mean starting again.
sparks.apply: Before your next big product decision, estimate how many customers exist in your chosen market and what they currently spend on this problem.

carousel.title: Count the actual buyers
carousel.body: Estimate how many organisations or people could realistically purchase, not the size of the industry a research firm describes in a headline.

carousel.title: Check what they spend today
carousel.body: Money already leaving their account for this problem is the clearest proof that a budget exists. A market with no current spending has to be created first.

carousel.title: Check the direction
carousel.body: A market shrinking slowly can look comfortable for years and then remove your whole business. Growth covers a great many execution mistakes; decline hides none.

carousel.title: Check you can reach them
carousel.body: Ask how you would contact a thousand of these buyers next month. A market you cannot address cheaply is somebody else's opportunity, not yours.

sparks.hook: This is a correlation study on a hand-built dataset. Read it that way.
sparks.insight: The comparison is far more rigorous than the anecdotes it replaces, and it is still not causal evidence. The company list was assembled by one investor, the control group required judgement calls to construct, the attributes were coded by hand, and none of it went through peer review. It also only covers companies that raised venture money, which excludes most businesses in the world. Treat the findings as a strong corrective to folklore rather than as a formula for predicting anything.
sparks.why: Descriptive comparison can rule things out convincingly while proving very little about what causes success. Rarity plus a small number of extreme outcomes makes statistical inference genuinely hard here.
sparks.apply: Use these findings to remove reasons you are not starting, and refuse to use them to predict whether a specific company will work.

sparks.hook: Use the data to disqualify fewer people, starting with yourself.
sparks.insight: The practical value of all this is negative rather than positive. It does not tell you who will build an enormous company, because nothing does. It does dismantle the reasons people give for not trying and the reasons investors give for passing: wrong age, no co-founder, not technical, not first, no famous degree. Each of those filters removes real candidates on evidence that does not hold up, which is expensive for the person filtered out and for whoever is doing the filtering.
sparks.why: Screening criteria with no predictive power still shape who gets funded, because they are easy to apply and they feel like judgement. That is how a whole industry can be systematically wrong for a long time.
sparks.apply: Write down every reason you think you are not the right person to start this. Cross out the ones this data contradicts, and address whatever is left.

actions: List the reasons you have given yourself for not starting, then mark each as either contradicted by the evidence here or a real gap you can close this year.
Estimate the size of your chosen market in customers and current spending, and treat that number as the ceiling on everything else you do.
Interview five customers of your nearest competitor about what still frustrates them, and turn the sharpest complaint into your positioning.
Identify one capability your first year genuinely requires, and decide explicitly whether to co-found, hire or contract for it.
books.not_for_you_if: You are building a small or bootstrapped business. The entire dataset is drawn from venture-funded companies chasing extreme outcomes, and little of it transfers.

verification.notes: Published 2021 by PublicAffairs. Tamaseb is a venture investor; the dataset is self-assembled and not peer reviewed, which the book itself acknowledges. Prose original.

books.title: The Cold Start Problem
books.subtitle: How to Start and Scale Network Effects
books.author: Andrew Chen
books.why_it_matters: Network effects were treated as a mystical property that either appeared or did not. This breaks them into a lifecycle with named stages and specific tactics, drawing on how marketplaces and social products were actually launched.

crux.headline: Do not launch a network. Launch one tiny network that works
crux.body: A product whose value comes from other users is worthless on day one, and no amount of marketing fixes an empty room. The escape is to ignore the market entirely and build the smallest group that is genuinely useful to itself: one campus, one office, one neighbourhood on one night. Get that group self-sustaining, then repeat it. Networks grow by copying a working cell, not by broadcasting to everyone at once.

sparks.hook: A network product is worthless on the day you launch it.
sparks.insight: Anything whose value comes from other people using it starts at zero and stays there until enough of them arrive. The first user of a messaging app has nobody to message. The first driver has no riders. This is not a marketing problem and cannot be spent past, because paid users arrive into an empty room and leave. Every successful network product got past this somehow, usually with tactics that look ridiculous at scale, and copying the mature version of a network tells you nothing about how it began.
sparks.why: Value depends on participation, so the product genuinely is bad early. Ordinary growth tactics assume the product already delivers value on arrival, which is precisely what is missing here.
sparks.apply: Write down what a single new user experiences if nobody else joins that week. If the answer is nothing, your first job is density rather than reach.

sparks.hook: Find the smallest group that would be useful to itself.
sparks.insight: The unit that matters is not the market, it is the smallest collection of people that keeps working without any help from you. For a workplace tool that might be one team of five in one office. For a ride service it might be a handful of drivers covering a few square miles on a Friday night. Get one of those to stability and you have proof plus a template. Aiming at a city or an industry from the start spreads your users so thinly that no group anywhere ever reaches the density that makes the product good.
sparks.why: Network value is local rather than global. A million scattered users can each have an empty experience, while a few hundred concentrated in one place have a working product.
sparks.apply: Define your smallest self-sustaining unit in one sentence with a place and a number in it, then pour everything into filling exactly one of them.

sparks.hook: Every network has a hard side, and it is not the one you count.
sparks.insight: Networks are lopsided. A small minority does most of the work that makes the thing valuable: the drivers, the hosts, the sellers, the people who actually post. That group is harder to recruit, harder to keep and usually has better alternatives. Yet product effort tends to flow to the easy side, because those users are numerous and their metrics move. Ask who does the work in your network, then build for them first, pay them properly and make their job easier before you optimise anything else.
sparks.why: Supply-side participants have higher switching flexibility and higher effort costs, so they defect faster. Losing them collapses the value proposition for everybody else almost immediately.
sparks.apply: Name the hard side of your network in one word, then find the single most tedious part of their experience and fix it this month.

sparks.hook: Give people a reason to show up before the network exists.
sparks.insight: A common escape from the empty room is to ship something useful to a single person alone, then let the network form on top of it. Photo filters were worth having before anybody followed you. A calendar or a document editor is useful before your colleagues join. The tool creates a reason to arrive and a reason to return, and the network quietly assembles in the background. The tool has to be genuinely good on its own, though, or you are simply describing an empty product with a slogan attached.
sparks.why: Single-player value removes the dependency on other users during the period when there are none, which is exactly when a network product is at its weakest.
sparks.apply: Design one feature that is worth using when the user is completely alone, and make it the first thing they encounter on signup.

sparks.hook: Fake the supply by hand until real supply turns up.
sparks.insight: Many networks were bootstrapped with work that looks nothing like software. Founders posted the first listings themselves, drove the first cars, staffed the first requests, copied content from elsewhere, or simply stood in the street recruiting. It is unglamorous, unscalable and entirely legitimate, because the alternative is a product that never demonstrates its value to anyone. The trap is being unwilling to do it. Founders who insist the system must work on its own from day one usually get a system that works for nobody.
sparks.why: Manual supply substitutes founder labour for network density during the period when density cannot exist. It becomes a problem only when nobody plans the handover to real participants.
sparks.apply: Choose one side of your network and supply it yourself for the next two weeks, with a written date for when real participants must take over.

carousel.title: Pick one side to fake
carousel.body: Decide which side of the network you will personally supply. Usually it is the hard side, because that is the one nobody joins voluntarily into an empty room.

carousel.title: Do it embarrassingly manually
carousel.body: Post the listings, make the calls, deliver the service yourself. Every awkward part you hit is a specification for what the product eventually has to automate.

carousel.title: Concentrate it in one place
carousel.body: Put all of your manual effort into a single network unit rather than spreading it. Density in one location beats a thin presence across ten of them.

carousel.title: Set a handover date
carousel.body: Write down when real participants must replace you and what threshold proves it. Without that date the manual work quietly becomes the business model.

sparks.hook: Grow by copying a working network, not by adding users.
sparks.insight: Once one small network works, growth becomes a repeatable operation rather than a marketing budget. You go to the next campus, the next city, the next company, and reproduce the same conditions that made the first one succeed. This is why network businesses launch geographically and why their playbooks read like field manuals. It also gives you a real test: if a second unit fails using the same method, you have not yet understood why the first one worked.
sparks.why: Replication converts a lucky success into a process. It also isolates variables, since a unit that fails in a new place reveals which local conditions the original success quietly depended on.
sparks.apply: Write down the exact conditions present when your first network unit succeeded, then attempt to reproduce all of them in a second unit.

sparks.hook: Sustained growth needs three loops running, not one growth hack.
sparks.insight: Fast growth in a network product comes from loops that feed themselves. The acquisition loop means existing users bring new ones, through invitations, shared content or visible use. The engagement loop means the product gives people reasons to return without a prompt from you. The economic loop means the money earned from users funds acquiring more of them. Any one loop alone stalls. Together they compound, and the job of a growth team is to find which of the three is currently broken.
sparks.why: Loops compound where campaigns do not. A channel spends money once for each customer, while a loop uses the output of the last cycle as the input to the next.
sparks.apply: Draw your three loops on one page and mark where each breaks. Fix the broken link rather than adding a fourth acquisition channel.

carousel.title: Acquisition loop
carousel.body: Users bring users, through invitations, shared content or visible public use. If new arrivals come only from paid channels, you have a funnel and not a loop.

carousel.title: Engagement loop
carousel.body: Something the network produces gives people a reason to come back on their own. Notifications count only when the thing they announce is genuinely worth returning for.

carousel.title: Economic loop
carousel.body: Revenue from existing users pays to bring in more. If each new customer costs more than they will ever return, growth is a countdown rather than a strategy.

sparks.hook: Every acquisition channel decays. Assume yours is already decaying.
sparks.insight: A channel that works well attracts everybody else, audiences get saturated, and response rates fall. This happens to banner ads, email, referral schemes, social feeds and whatever is currently working for you. It means growth teams are never finished, and it means a company that built its whole model on one cheap channel has a hidden expiry date. Plan for channel decay in the same way you plan for equipment wearing out, rather than treating each decline as a failure of execution.
sparks.why: Channels degrade because attention is finite and competitors copy anything that works. The decline is structural, so it continues regardless of how well your team executes.
sparks.apply: Chart the cost per acquisition of your main channel over the past year. If the line is rising, start testing a second channel now.

sparks.hook: Networks stop growing for reasons your team cannot work harder at.
sparks.insight: Growth eventually slows and the internal instinct is to blame effort. Usually the causes are structural. The easiest users have already joined, so each new one is harder to reach. Scale attracts spam and low-quality participants, which degrades the experience for everyone. Crowding makes the network less useful, as anybody who has watched a feed fill with noise knows. Recognising a ceiling for what it is changes the response from pushing harder to changing the product.
sparks.why: Saturation, quality degradation and overcrowding are properties of large networks rather than symptoms of poor management. They arrive on schedule for products that are working exactly as designed.
sparks.apply: Split your growth curve by cohort and by segment to find which specific group has stalled, then treat that as a product problem rather than a marketing one.

sparks.hook: The big launch is the wrong weapon against a network incumbent.
sparks.insight: Attacking an established network with an enormous simultaneous launch tends to fail, even with a great deal of money behind it. Everyone arrives at once into a product with no local density, finds nobody they know, and leaves. The approach that works is to find an edge of the incumbent's network where the experience is bad or a group they serve poorly, take that segment properly, and grow inward. Networks are beaten at their weakest corner, not at their strongest point.
sparks.why: Mass launches spread users too thinly for any single group to reach density, so the product feels empty precisely when curiosity is highest and first impressions are being formed.
sparks.apply: Identify one group your dominant competitor serves badly and build a product that is unmistakably the best option for that group alone.

actions: Define your atomic network in one sentence that includes a place and a number, then concentrate all acquisition effort on filling exactly one of them.
Name the hard side of your network and spend a week doing their job yourself, listing every friction point you encounter along the way.
Draw your acquisition, engagement and economic loops on a single page, mark where each one breaks, and fix the weakest link before adding a channel.
Chart cost per acquisition for your main channel across the last twelve months and begin testing an alternative if the trend is upward.
books.not_for_you_if: Your product delivers full value to a single user with no one else involved. Most of this concerns problems your business will never have.

verification.notes: Published 2021 by Harper Business. Chen is a venture investor and formerly led growth at Uber. Prose here is original.

books.title: The Startup Owner's Manual
books.subtitle: The Step-by-Step Guide for Building a Great Company
books.author: Steve Blank and Bob Dorf
books.why_it_matters: The full checklist version of customer development, the method that gave the lean startup movement its engine. Nearly every accelerator curriculum in the world is a compressed version of what is set out here.

crux.headline: A startup is a search party, not a small company
crux.body: An established company executes a business model it already understands. A startup has only a stack of guesses about who the customer is, what hurts, and what they will pay. Confusing the two makes you build the wrong thing efficiently. Organise to search instead: numbered assumptions, cheap tests run by the founders themselves, and a rule that failing a test sends you backwards rather than forwards.

sparks.hook: A startup is not a small company. It is a search party.
sparks.insight: A company executes a business model it already knows. A startup does not have one yet — it has a set of guesses about who the customer is, what problem they have, and what they will pay. Confusing the two is the most expensive mistake in early business. If you organise like a company, with a sales target, a launch date and a functional org chart, you will spend the money building the wrong thing very efficiently. Organise to search instead: cheap experiments, fast rewrites, no permanent structures.
sparks.why: The failure mode is structural rather than personal. Execution machinery makes commitments hard to reverse, and a search phase needs everything to stay reversible until the model is proven.
sparks.apply: Write your business model as a list of numbered guesses. Mark the one that kills everything if it is wrong, and go and test that one first.

sparks.hook: There are no facts inside your building. Go outside and get some.
sparks.insight: Everything inside the office is opinion dressed as analysis: your roadmap, your persona document, your pricing, your competitive matrix. The facts live with the people who might pay you, and the only way to get them is to sit in front of those people repeatedly and ask. Founders have to do this themselves rather than hiring a research agency, because the point is not the report. The point is that the person deciding what to build has heard a customer be unimpressed, in their own voice.
sparks.why: Second-hand research strips out the tone, the hesitation and the ugly workaround the customer has already built, which is usually where the actual product is hiding.
sparks.apply: Book five conversations this week with people who fit your target customer, and ask about their current workaround before you describe your product at all.

sparks.hook: Four steps stand between a guess and a company that can scale.
sparks.insight: Customer development runs in a fixed order, and skipping ahead is why startups explode. First you discover whether the problem and the customer are real. Then you validate that you can sell the solution repeatedly, yourself, at a price that works. Only then do you spend on creating demand, and only after that do you convert the search team into a functioning organisation. Each step has an exit test, and failing it sends you backwards rather than forwards. That backwards move is what a pivot actually is.
sparks.why: The order encodes cost. Every step forward multiplies your burn rate, so proving the cheap things first is what keeps a wrong answer survivable rather than terminal.
sparks.apply: Identify which of the four steps you are honestly in right now, then stop any spending that properly belongs to a later step.

carousel.title: Discover the problem
carousel.body: Turn your assumptions into testable statements and take them to real customers. You are looking for a problem people already spend time or money trying to solve badly.

carousel.title: Validate the sale
carousel.body: Sell to strangers with the founders doing the selling. If you cannot close repeatedly without heroics, you have not found a business model yet, only interest.

carousel.title: Create demand
carousel.body: Now spend on marketing to pull buyers into the funnel. How much you spend and how you spend it depends entirely on which kind of market you are entering.

carousel.title: Build the company
carousel.body: Only once the model repeats do you replace the search team with departments, process and the ordinary machinery of execution.

sparks.hook: The kind of market you enter changes every number in your plan.
sparks.insight: Entering an existing market is a race on features against known rivals, and customers already understand what you sell. Creating a new market means nobody is searching for you, adoption takes years, and your early budget goes on education rather than competition. Resegmenting means carving a niche or a cheaper position inside somebody else's market. Cloning means bringing a proven model to a new country. These paths have completely different spending curves, and borrowing the wrong one's plan is a reliable way to die on schedule.
sparks.why: Market type determines when revenue can plausibly arrive. New-market companies that budget like existing-market companies run out of cash during the education phase, which was always the expected phase.
sparks.apply: Name your market type in one word, then rebuild your first three years of forecasts around its adoption curve rather than a competitor's.

sparks.hook: Your first customers should already be trying to fix this themselves.
sparks.insight: The best early buyers are not the ones who enjoy your demo. They are people who have the problem, know they have it, have gone looking for a solution, and have already improvised something ugly — a spreadsheet, a manual process, three tools taped together. That improvisation is the strongest evidence of demand you will ever get, and it also means they will tolerate your unfinished product, because their current alternative is worse. Selling to anyone earlier on that ladder means doing the customer's realising for them.
sparks.why: Awareness of a problem is a prerequisite for buying. A customer who has not yet built a workaround is telling you the pain has not reached the threshold where money moves.
sparks.apply: For each prospect, ask what they do about this problem today. Deprioritise anyone whose honest answer is that they do nothing at all.

sparks.hook: A pivot is a change to the model, not a change of mind.
sparks.insight: The word gets used for any wobble, which makes it useless. Use it precisely: a pivot is a substantive change to one component of the business model — the customer, the problem, the channel, the pricing, the value proposition — made because a test told you the current version is wrong. That definition has teeth. It means a pivot requires a failed test to justify it, it means you change one component and re-test rather than rebuilding everything, and it means constant pivoting is a sign you are not testing at all.
sparks.why: Naming the specific component stops you discarding the parts that were working. Most failed pivots throw away validated learning along with the broken assumption, and start again from zero.
sparks.apply: Before your next big change, write down which single component of the model is changing and what evidence forced it. If you cannot, it is not a pivot.

sparks.hook: Do not hire a salesperson until you have sold it yourself.
sparks.insight: Founders often treat selling as beneath them and hire a sales team to find out whether the product sells. It never works, because the first sales are not a sales job. They are research that happens to produce revenue. Until you know who buys, which objection kills the deal, what creates urgency and what price sticks, there is no roadmap for a salesperson to follow, so you are asking somebody to execute a process nobody has discovered. Sell it yourself until the sale is boringly repeatable.
sparks.why: An early sales hire fails for structural reasons and then looks like a bad hire. The company loses a year and frequently concludes, wrongly, that the market was the problem.
sparks.apply: Set an explicit threshold before your first sales hire, such as ten closed deals you personally ran using the same pitch and the same price.

sparks.hook: Build the smallest thing capable of proving you wrong.
sparks.insight: A minimum viable product is not a cheap version of the finished product. It is an instrument for answering one question you currently cannot answer, built to the lowest fidelity that still gives a trustworthy answer. Sometimes that means working software, and often it means a page, a document, a demo or a service you perform by hand. The test of a good one is not whether customers like it but whether their reaction changes what you do next. If every outcome leaves your plan unchanged, you built the wrong instrument.
sparks.why: Cost per experiment sets how many wrong guesses you can survive. Anything in the build that does not serve the current question is money you will not get back.
sparks.apply: Write the question your next build answers, plus the two possible results and the different action each would trigger, before anyone writes code.

carousel.title: State the question
carousel.body: Name the single uncertainty that matters most right now, phrased so that it can come back false. Vague questions produce builds that cannot fail and therefore cannot teach.

carousel.title: Pick the cheapest instrument
carousel.body: Choose the lowest-fidelity thing that would still convince you: a landing page, a manual service, a clickable mock. Fidelity costs money and rarely changes the answer.

carousel.title: Set the threshold first
carousel.body: Decide before the test what result counts as a pass. Deciding afterwards guarantees you will find some way to read the data as encouraging.

carousel.title: Run it on strangers
carousel.body: Test with people who have no relationship with you. Friends and advisers give you politeness, which is indistinguishable from demand right up until you invoice.

carousel.title: Act on the answer
carousel.body: Write down the decision the result forces and take it within the week. An experiment nobody acts on is an expensive kind of procrastination.

sparks.hook: Failing a checkpoint sends you backwards. That is the system working.
sparks.insight: Every stage of customer development has an exit condition, and if you do not meet it the instruction is to go back, not to press on with a smaller version of the same plan. That is uncomfortable, because backwards looks like failure to everybody watching, investors included. But the alternative is scaling a model you have not proven, which converts a recoverable setback into an unrecoverable one. Startups that die have usually passed a checkpoint they had actually failed.
sparks.why: The cost of continuing rises steeply at each step, so an unproven assumption carried forward gets more expensive the longer it goes unexamined, and harder to admit to.
sparks.apply: Define the pass condition for your current stage in one measurable sentence, and agree with your co-founders in advance what happens if you miss it.

sparks.hook: This is a manual, not a book. Use it like one.
sparks.insight: It runs to several hundred pages of checklists and is close to unreadable cover to cover, which is a format rather than a flaw. Used properly you open it at the stage you are in, follow the specific list for that stage, and close it again. That makes it far more useful as a shared reference for a founding team than as something one person reads alone. The checklist form also imposes a real discipline: it is much harder to pretend you completed a step when the step has a list attached.
sparks.why: Checklists work by removing reliance on memory and optimism, the same reason they hold up in aviation and surgery. Their weakness is that they invite box-ticking in place of judgement.
sparks.apply: Print the checklist for the single stage you are actually in, put it on the wall, and review it with your co-founder every Friday.

actions: Write your business model out as numbered assumptions, rank them by how fatal each would be if wrong, and design a cheap test for the top three this month.
Do ten customer conversations yourself, with no slides, asking only about how they handle the problem today and what that workaround costs them.
Name your market type in writing and rebuild your revenue forecast around the adoption curve that type implies, not the one your pitch deck wants.
Agree a written pass condition for your current stage with your co-founders, including what you will do if the condition is not met.
books.not_for_you_if: You want an evening read or a narrative. This is a dense reference volume of checklists, and reading it straight through will exhaust you well before it helps you.

verification.notes: Published 2012 by K&S Ranch. Expands the customer development method Blank first set out in 2005. Prose here is original.

books.title: An Elegant Puzzle
books.subtitle: Systems of Engineering Management
books.author: Will Larson
books.why_it_matters: It treats management as a systems problem with measurable stocks, flows and delays rather than a people-skills problem, which is why it survives contact with a real organisation. It remains the reference text for anyone running engineering teams at scale.

crux.headline: Manage the system, not the individual incidents
crux.body: Most management problems recur because they are produced by a structure rather than by the people caught inside it. Teams are the unit that matters, not individuals. Their size, their state of health, how work arrives and how debt accumulates all obey rules you can reason about. Once you see the org as a system with inputs, delays and feedback loops, the daily crises stop looking like separate emergencies and start looking like symptoms with a small number of underlying causes.

sparks.hook: Adding people to a struggling team usually makes it slower for months.
sparks.insight: The reflex when a team is drowning is to hire. But new people consume the capacity of the existing ones for a quarter or more before they contribute, so if the team is merely overloaded rather than genuinely under-resourced, hiring makes the next three months worse. What a stretched team usually needs is fewer things in flight, so it can finish something. What a permanently under-resourced team needs is people. Diagnosing which situation you are in is the whole decision.
sparks.why: Onboarding has a real, front-loaded cost paid by the people already there. That cost is invisible in a headcount plan, which is why hiring gets applied to problems it cannot solve.
sparks.apply: Before requesting headcount, cut your team's concurrent projects in half for six weeks and see whether throughput recovers on its own.

sparks.hook: Every team is in one of four states, and each needs a different fix.
sparks.insight: Teams are not simply good or bad. A team can be falling behind, where the backlog grows faster than it shrinks. It can be treading water, keeping the critical work alive but never getting ahead. It can be actively repaying accumulated debt. Or it can be innovating, with slack to spend on new things. Each state has one appropriate intervention and applying the wrong one wastes a quarter. You also cannot skip states: an overwhelmed team has to pass through the middle two before it can innovate.
sparks.why: The states form a sequence rather than a menu, which is why interventions that worked for one team fail for another that looks superficially similar but sits at a different point.
sparks.apply: Place each team you own into one of the four states this week, then apply only the matching intervention for the next quarter.

carousel.title: Falling behind: add people
carousel.body: The queue grows faster than the team can clear it and morale is dropping. This is the one situation where hiring genuinely is the answer, and it takes a quarter to land.

carousel.title: Treading water: cut the work
carousel.body: Critical things get done and nothing improves. Reduce concurrent projects hard so the team can finish something, because finishing is what creates the room to get ahead.

carousel.title: Repaying debt: add time
carousel.body: The team is fixing the foundations. Protect the schedule and resist the urge to inject new work; this stage looks unproductive from outside and is the one that pays for everything after it.

carousel.title: Innovating: leave them alone
carousel.body: There is slack, the backlog is short, and new work is being invented. Your job here is to defend the slack against the constant pressure to consume it.

sparks.hook: The team is the unit of work. Individuals are just where it happens.
sparks.insight: Organisations that assign projects to individuals get brittleness: knowledge concentrates in one head, the work stops when that person leaves, and nobody can take a holiday. Assigning ownership to teams instead is slower to feel productive and vastly more durable. It also changes how you plan. You stop trying to match a specific person to a specific task and start asking whether a team has a coherent area, enough people to sustain it, and a clear boundary with the teams next to it.
sparks.why: Team-level ownership survives turnover, illness and promotion; individual ownership does not. The cost is a short-term loss of the efficiency that comes from always using the best-matched person.
sparks.apply: List every critical system you own and name the team that owns it. Anything owned by a single person is a risk to be fixed this quarter.

sparks.hook: Teams below six are fragile. Above ten they need another manager.
sparks.insight: Team size is not a matter of taste. Below roughly six people, a team cannot sustain an on-call rotation, absorb a departure, or take a holiday without stalling, so it stays permanently anxious. Above roughly ten, a manager can no longer hold real context on each person's work and coordination overhead starts eating the gains from having more people. The band in between is where most teams work well, and drifting outside it produces problems that get misdiagnosed as culture or motivation.
sparks.why: Both limits come from concrete constraints: rotation coverage and resilience at the bottom, the manager's attention and communication paths at the top. Neither depends on how good the people are.
sparks.apply: Count the members of every team you own. Merge anything under five and split anything over ten, planning both moves this quarter.

sparks.hook: Migrations are the only way large systems ever pay down debt.
sparks.insight: Beyond a certain size, technical debt cannot be cleaned up incrementally, because the rate of new debt matches the rate you fix it. The only mechanism that changes the picture is a full migration: everything moves to the new approach and the old one is genuinely removed. Half-finished migrations are worse than none at all, because you now maintain two systems and every engineer must learn both. That means the deciding question is not whether the new approach is better but whether you will actually finish.
sparks.why: Partial migration leaves permanent duplicate cost, so the ability to complete matters more than the quality of the destination. Most organisations underestimate the tail of the work by a wide margin.
sparks.apply: List your unfinished migrations, pick the one closest to completion, and staff it until it is finished before starting anything new.

sparks.hook: Write policy for the common case and treat exceptions as exceptions.
sparks.insight: Managers make two opposite mistakes with rules. One is deciding everything case by case, which is exhausting, inconsistent and rewards whoever argues hardest. The other is writing a policy so comprehensive it covers every edge case and nobody can read it. The workable middle is a short policy that handles the ordinary situation well, plus an explicit route for exceptions that a named person approves. Exceptions handled openly are fine. Exceptions granted quietly are how a policy dies.
sparks.why: A policy exists to remove repeated decisions, so complexity defeats its own purpose. Making the exception path visible is what keeps the rule credible for everyone who did not get one.
sparks.apply: Take your most contested recurring decision, write a policy for the common case in under a page, and name who approves exceptions.

sparks.hook: You cannot mandate a change sideways. You can make it obvious.
sparks.insight: Most of the changes an engineering leader wants involve people they do not manage. Instructions do not work there, and neither does arguing in meetings. What does work is a sequence: build the thing yourself so it demonstrably exists, write down clearly how and why it works, and only then invite others to adopt it. Each step lowers the cost of the next person saying yes. Attempting the last step first is why so many good technical proposals die in a review committee.
sparks.why: Adoption without authority depends on lowering risk for the adopter. A working example plus documentation removes most of that risk; a proposal document alone removes none of it.
sparks.apply: Pick one change you have been arguing for, stop arguing, build a working version in one team, and write up what happened.

carousel.title: Build it somewhere real
carousel.body: Implement the change in one team, ideally your own, and run it long enough to hit the problems. A working example ends most of the theoretical objections by itself.

carousel.title: Write down what happened
carousel.body: Document the approach, the results and the parts that went badly. Including the failures is what makes the write-up credible to people who did not choose this.

carousel.title: Make adoption cheap
carousel.body: Provide the templates, tooling or migration script so the next team spends hours rather than weeks. Adoption cost is usually the real objection behind a stated one.

carousel.title: Let it spread, then standardise
carousel.body: Once several teams have chosen it, make it the default. Standardising before there is evidence turns a good idea into an imposed one people work around.

sparks.hook: A career ladder is mostly a device for reducing arguments about promotion.
sparks.insight: Without written levels, promotion decisions get made on visibility, advocacy and who is closest to a decision-maker, and everyone can feel it even when nobody can prove it. A ladder that describes observable behaviour at each level does not remove judgement, but it moves the argument to a shared document instead of a private one. It also makes the manager's job easier: instead of defending a decision, you point at the gap between what somebody does and what the next level describes.
sparks.why: Legible criteria reduce the influence of proximity and self-promotion on advancement. The ladder is imperfect and gameable; the undocumented alternative is worse and less fair.
sparks.apply: Write one paragraph of observable behaviour for each level on your team, share it, and use it in your next promotion discussion.

sparks.hook: Interviewing is expensive engineering time nobody puts on the plan.
sparks.insight: Every interview loop consumes several hours from people who were otherwise building things, plus the recovery time around it. Organisations rarely count this, so they run wasteful processes and then wonder why delivery slipped during a hiring push. Counting it changes decisions: you shorten loops, you stop interviewing for roles you are not going to fill, and you concentrate interviewing among people who are good at it rather than spreading it evenly as a tax on everyone.
sparks.why: Unmeasured costs are always overspent. Making interview hours visible turns hiring into a resourcing decision rather than an invisible drain on the same teams under delivery pressure.
sparks.apply: Total your team's interview hours for last month, put the number in your capacity plan, and cut one stage from the loop.

sparks.hook: Do the work that only you can do. Give away the rest, even the fun parts.
sparks.insight: Every manager has a set of tasks that they alone can perform: the organisational decisions, the conversations that require your authority, the strategy nobody else has the context to write. Around that sits a much larger set of work you happen to be good at and enjoy. Holding onto the second set is understandable, since it is where you feel competent, and it is also what stops your team growing. The test is not whether you do it well. It is whether anyone else could.
sparks.why: Doing work others could do has a hidden cost: it removes their development opportunity and occupies the time your unique work needed. Both costs land later, which is why the trade feels free now.
sparks.apply: List everything you did last week, mark each as only-you or someone-else, and hand over the largest someone-else item this month.

actions: Place every team you own into one of the four states and apply only the matching intervention for a full quarter.
